sections.title: Social Justice and Public Scholarship -- Labor and Documentation in Asian Diasporic NYC
sections.description:
This course introduces students to the intersections of public scholarship and social justice through the lens of Asian diasporic communities in New York City, with particular attention to labor organizing and working-class Asian communities.

Interdisciplinary by design, students examine, analyze, and reflect on a range of scholars, artists, and activists who are committed to the vision of a more just world through their community-engaged, or public-facing work. Drawing on methodologies in ethnography, participatory action research, public art projects and community-based archiving, the course pays special attention to how race, ethnicity, gender, class, and immigration status converge in the workplace and in the archive.

Case studies may include oral histories and art installations from Red Canary Song, participatory action research surveys used by the New York Taxi Workers Alliance and art projection and ‘placekeeping’ mapping used by Chinatown Art Brigade. We will also examine collections at the New York Public Library and Interference Archives.

A central concern of the course will be the role of community documentation — from the mundane recounting of work tasks to the creation of worker education programs to the narratives formed through oral histories — to labor struggles in general. By the end of the course, students will learn how to design and put into practice the framework for a successful and non-extractive public-facing, and/ or community-engaged research project.

sections.title: Foodways of the Middle East and North Africa: Culture, Politics, Sustainability
sections.description:
This seminar explores the social, cultural, and political dimensions of food and foodways across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and its global diasporas. Moving from foundational social science theories of taste, value, waste, and political ecology, the course investigates how culinary practices intersect with state formation, gendered labor, colonial legacies, and transnational mobility. Central to our inquiry is the concept of culinary nationalism and gastro-diplomacy, examining how everyday staples like hummus, falafel, and couscous become sites of geopolitical tension, heritage claims, and identity formation. Through a mix of recent ethnographic monographs, historical analyses, critical food studies literature, and popular media (including cookbooks), we will analyze how food functions simultaneously as a sensory experience, a commodity chain, and a political battleground.

The second half of the semester addresses pressing contemporary crises facing the region, including food sovereignty versus state-managed food security, the political economy of bread, climate vulnerability, water scarcity, and urban food waste. To bridge theoretical frameworks with lived experience, the course incorporates an active fieldwork component in New York City. Students will engage with local MENA foodways across the five boroughs through critical menu analyses, grocery store supply-chain mapping, and semi-structured ethnographic interviews with migrant vendors, restaurant workers, and community members.

Designed for master’s and doctoral students in anthropology, Middle Eastern studies, sociology, history, and food studies, this seminar equips students with the theoretical and methodological tools necessary to conduct original, field-based research on the gastro-politics of the region and its diasporic nodes.

sections.title: US Imperial Crisis and the Horizons of Emancipation
sections.description: What kind of critical work on the United States should scholars produce to defend precarious lives amidst an ongoing US imperial crisis? How might we advance political stances that illuminate the horizons of emancipation and contribute to the end of oppression, violence, and exploitation in all their forms? This course seeks to address these questions by foregrounding recent contributions from American studies, Black diasporic studies, critical ethnic studies, Native studies, literary studies, anthropology, and history on the relations of capitalism and colonialism through which the United States is produced and reproduced as a concrete social formation. Working to unsettle the methodological nationalism and American exceptionalism that are hallmarks of conventional American accounts, we seek instead to reconsider "the United States" by treating it as a problematic, contradiction-laden space concealing global operations of colonial and imperial power. We will work together to uncover the death-dealing logics and practices that define the contemporary imperial crisis. And we will explore the substance and limits of abolitionist and other counter-hegemonic political projects, asking what they demand of us as engaged scholars and how their emancipatory horizons must change to address the shifting dynamics of imperial decline.

sections.title: Language and Political Subjectivity
sections.description: This seminar investigates the dynamic processes through which political subjects and linguistic practices are mutually constituted. Moving beyond the view of language as a mere reflection of the social structure, we examine how discourse and communicative action are foundational to political consciousness, stancemaking, and the contestation of power. Reading across linguistic anthropology, political theory, cultural sociology, and ethnographic cases from diverse political, historical, and cultural contexts, the course traces an analytical trajectory from the micro-politics of interaction and bodily habits to macro-regimes of institutional hegemony. In doing so, we examine how regulatory regimes of standardization clash with vernacular and poetic resistance; how convictions and the risks of speaking truth to power are corporeally sustained; and how narrative testimony is mobilized across social movements, state archives, and human rights courts. The seminar provides a critical framework for analyzing how meaning is interactionally achieved and institutionally disciplined in the ongoing reproduction and transformation of political life.

sections.title: Nycep
sections.description: This course provides students an opportunity to learn about, discuss, and gain practical experience in many of the professional, practical, and ethical issues that confront scholars in biological anthropology. This includes issues related to ethics in research, training, and publication as well as practical training in some of the oral presentation and writing skills that students will find essential in their early academic careers.

sections.title: Core Course in Evolutionary Morphology
sections.description: This course introduces students to primate skeletal morphology from an evolutionary perspective. Students will examine skeletal elements of extant primates as well as fossils and will focus on aspects of cranial, dental, postcranial, and some soft tissue anatomy of extant primates, with background on primate systematics, adaptation and evolution and on the morphological diversity within groups of extant primates

sections.title: Special Topics in Genocide, Mass Violence, and Crimes Against Humanity
sections.description: This seminar takes a critical look at carceral regimes in Africa, Asia, Latin America, North America, Europe and Australia in the past and present. We will explore carceral regimes through fiction, prison memoirs, testimony, ethnography, legal, policy, anthropological and other academic literature on imprisonment, detention and disappearance as State processes of domination and exclusion. One of our goals is to understand the ways in which carceral regimes and the official creation of historical truth(s) as well as definitions of crime and punishment reaffirm hegemonic structures and gendered Eurocentric colonial practices of exclusion and inequality.

sections.title: Critical Agrarian Studies
sections.description:
Critical Agrarian Studies — like Critical Legal Studies and Critical Race Theory — represents a rethinking and upending of conventional paradigms, in this case those emanating from the World Bank and mainstream policy and academic institutions concerned with rural development and rural people. Like these other critical approaches, it involves networks of scholar-activists, academic journals and institutions, and civil society movements and researchers. Geographically it spans the Americas, Asia, Africa, and Europe. This course will introduce key debates in Critical Agrarian Studies, including:

· Debates over rural differentiation (Lenin versus Chayanov versus Bukharin) and the real-world consequences of the polemics over the emergence of social classes in the Russian countryside, as well as the echoes of these debates in Latin America and elsewhere in the mid- to late 20th century.

· Agrarian social classes and the origins of dictatorship and democracy. A reconsideration after 60 years of Barrington Moore’s famous thesis and its implications for understanding contemporary authoritarianism.

· Revolutionary and conservative sectors of the peasantry. Eric Wolf’s “middle peasant” thesis versus Jeffery Paige’s “poor peasant” thesis.

· State- versus market-led land reform in the 20th and early 21st century. The role of agrarian reform in East Asia’s dynamic capitalism and the reasons why East Asia surpassed Latin America in development terms. The efforts to achieve gender equity in agrarian reform and the impacts of gender relations in agrarian counter-reform and struggles against it.

· The successive British-centered, U.S. and corporate “food regimes” and the transitions between them. The battles over the future of farming, climate mitigation (e.g., REDD+), seeds and intellectual property, and agricultural knowledge.

· Dispossession and the land rush in the Global South and North. The debates over “adverse incorporation,” the validity and usefulness of big data, and strategies to reverse land grabbing.

· The usefulness (or limitations) of analyzing capitalism through a commodity lens, with case studies of cotton (Sven Beckert) and palm oil (Max Haiven).

· New forms of resistance, such as “rightful protest” (O’Brien and Li, China), “not being governed” (James Scott, Southeast Asia), and transnational agrarian movements (e.g., La Vía Campesina and others).

sections.title: Seminar in Ethnomusicolgy: Field Methods in Ethnomusicology
Racial Alterities
sections.description: The making of rigid racial categories was paramount to colonial, capitalist projects. Anthropologists have long contributed to investigating how such worlds were and are made, as well as the modes through which racialized people resisted the violence of the racial order. At the same time, a growing body of literature challenges an overreliance on racial categories to understand the past or present, noting that doing so obscures the complexity of lived experience, reproduces partial or reductive interpretations, and ultimately reifies the very categories we seek to interrogate. This course will explore the making of racial worlds and encourage students to think through the permeability, inadequacy, and the breakdown of these categories. The course is primarily archaeological in nature, working to understand the material dimensions of race and its alterities, but we will draw from scholarship across anthropology and related disciplines.

Black Feminist Poetics & Aesthetics: “Becoming & Going: Under the Eyes of the Black Self”
sections.description: This course engages and explores literary and cultural production using Black Feminist poetic and aesthetic lenses. Students will examine different methods of thinking about Black feminist praxis as a site of inquiry/research. Our course theme, “becoming and going under the eyes of the black self” signifies the ways in which Black poetry symbolizes becoming, going, and defining the black self. Centering Black feminist theory/praxis and the concept of “symbolic voice” [identity/utterance/agency] as representative of the Black experience, struggle, and resistance, students will consider how Black women’s art and poetry is reflective of historical periods and cultural moments, the political and socio-economic circumstances of Black people, and expressions of agency and resistance. This course uses frameworks and concepts such as Black art, Black aesthetics, and Black feminist poetics/aesthetics to emphasize and situate the historical and cultural contexts that create and make-meaning of Black Feminist experience(s) and voice(s) as reflected in African Diasporic art, music, and poetry. Students will examine a cross-genre of texts (theory, fine art, poetry & hip-hop) across artistic, cultural, and literary movements.

sections.title: Interdisciplinary Theories and Research on Race and Ethnic Studies
sections.description: This seminar introduces major interdisciplinary theoretical perspectives that inform research and scholarship on race and ethnic studies in the U.S. and beyond. The seminar highlights the centrality of interdisciplinary, multidisciplinary, and transdisciplinary approaches to the study of race and ethnicity. It also examines the core concepts that have informed the field, including intersectionality, indigeneity, diaspora, transnationalism, racism, and decolonization. It also introduces core components of research design, including the politics and ethics of research, how to develop research projects, issues on sampling, measurement, and operationalization, and an introduction to the collection, management, and analysis of qualitative and quantitative data.

sections.title: Gender, Race, and Social Justice
sections.description: This interdisciplinary course examines how gender and race shape social experiences and inequalities in contemporary society. The course draws on concepts, theories, and current scholarship from a variety of disciplines, including sociology, criminology, criminal justice, gender studies, history, and economics. Topics may include mass incarceration and justice-involved women; gendered migration; sexual victimization and gender-based violence; drug use, mental illness, and the “War on Drugs” in the United States; educational inequality and achievement; reproductive rights; capitalism and labor markets; and contemporary social movements, among others. By the end of the course, students will gain a deeper understanding of major contemporary social problems and the ways in which race, gender, class, and other social identities shape individual experiences, life opportunities, and achievements. Students will learn to critically analyze social issues through an intersectional lens, evaluate current policies, and consider alternative approaches to promoting social justice, equality, and social change. The course will culminate in student presentations on topics of their choice related to gender, race, and social justice.

sections.description: During the late 20th century pathbreaking historians addressed slavery as a "problem" for western culture, for American exceptionalism, and even for the discipline of history itself. Now, no one would now say slavery is not at or near the center of what historians of the Atlantic world and of the early U.S. do, but what has been accomplished and what problems of interpretation remain?

sections.title: Africana Studies: Global Perspectives
sections.description: This course examines problems of existence and freedom posed by black life. We will explore how the racialization of people of African descent through the means of violence and oppression translates into an existential predicament addressing the human confrontation with hope and hopelessness, freedom, and human degradation, being and non-being. We will discuss the existentialist implications, challenges, and possibilities of black life in Africana literature, film, and music. How do cultural expressions of black people simultaneously engage being acted upon by the external forces of enslavement and racism, while acting against those forces? Through critical analyses of music, film, fiction, and contemporary events, this class will generate theoretical interventions embedded in the poetics and politics of (self) representation, freedom, and social constructions of black existence.

sections.title: Introduction to Global Modern and Contemporary Studies
sections.description: Colonialism and postcolonialism have profoundly shaped and continue to shape the modern and contemporary world. In this class, we will explore a range of case studies and theoretical pieces that ask questions about colonial and racial capitalism, indigeneity, gender and sexuality, carcerality, transnational organizing, social movements, borders, art, and other themes. We will focus on the experiences of marginalized and minoritized groups across the globe in order to understand the impact of colonial and settler colonial histories and legacies on their lives. We will also consider how the embodied axes of race, gender, class, sexuality, ability, and national origins determine the limits of material success, mental and physical well-being, access to healthcare and education, and struggle. The class will be organized thematically. Each week, we will examine a narrow set of questions that scholars have posed within a specific subfield through scholarly and creative writing as well as film and visual culture.

sections.title: Slavery and Social Status in Middle Eastern History
sections.description: In this class, we will explore social, political, economic, legal, and cultural aspects of slavery in premodern Islamic history. Starting in the late antique Mediterranean, we will consider the emergence of a variety of forms of slavery in the Islamic Middle East, including military slavery and agricultural slavery, but focus especially on the enslavement of women. We will end with the complex relationship between Islam and transatlantic slavery and various ethical and political implications of the history of religiously validated enslavement. We will consider a range of sources, including legal material and popular literature. Prior knowledge of Middle Eastern or Islamic history is not required.

sections.title: Demography, Politics, and Societies in the Middle East and North Africa
sections.description: The demographics of the Middle East show a highly populated, culturally diverse region spanning three continents. This course examines population trends and their implications for national and international politics and policies in the MENA region as well as their impact on social and cultural changes. Topics include demographic transitions, population growth and the environment, public health policies, gender and family patterns, control of fertility, mortality, forced and voluntary migration, boom and bust cycles, and graying of populations.

sections.title: Special Topics in Public Scholarship
sections.description: While there is a myriad of ways to do public scholarship, the GC holds a long radical tradition of research that is non-extractive, multidisciplinary, committed to the public good and rooted in Black Studies, Ethnic Studies and Queer Studies. Special Topics in Public Scholarship will honor these roots by exploring three interweaving public pillars of knowledge production: Oral Histories, Archives, and Zines. We will study the work of feminist BIPOC oral historians, explore the politics of creating archives, and look at how radical histories interweave with Black feminist zine making practice. Students will work on a collective oral history project, learn how to curate oral histories for various archives, and deepen their zine-making practice.

Asian American and Pacific Islanders are often an underexamined population in the United States. Yet their presence and histories have not only made contributions to the United States but were also fraught by discriminatory and racist laws. Select Asian ethnic group's successes after World War II have also been used to justify racialized stratification in the American imagination. This course takes an interdisciplinary examination of the critical issues in Asian American and diasporic communities. We will discuss Asian American and Pacific Islander migration and community histories, especially the relevant aspects missing from mainstream knowledge. Specifically, this course will cover major themes, such as historical and contemporary immigration laws, social movements, racialization theories, gendered experiences, comparative educational outcomes, and community politics.

sections.title: Thesis Writing Course
sections.description:
FOR MA STUDENTS WHO ARE WRITING OR JUST ABOUT TO WRITE CAPSTONE PROJECTS (You must have an advisor committed in order to sign up.)

The Thesis Writing Course - MALS 72000 is a three-credit research and writing course open to MALS students working on their theses. The course is designed to help students develop strategies for composing, drafting, and crafting their theses. Students will work on analyzing and synthesizing their materials in order to sharpen their approach to their scholarly topics. They will also work on developing their writing in logically framed and rhetorically convincing graduate-level prose. Students will produce multiple drafts, consider the best organizational approaches for their projects, develop and hone their authorial voices, develop strategies for building arguments that are supported by the evidence they have collected, and reflect upon their individual research and writing practices. Students will give and receive feedback from their peers as well as from the professor. Students normally have at least 18 credits when they are given permission to enroll in this course. Typically, students take MALS 72000 either the semester before they enroll in MALS 79000 or concurrent with MALS 79000.

If you would like to sign up for the thesis writing course, permission from the department is required. Please email Amber and Gabrielle with your name, thesis advisor and where you are in the process. This is a 3-credit course and it is not a substitute for BRES 79000.

sections.title: Proseminar in Classical Studies
sections.description:
This is an informative and “how to” proseminar designed to introduce students to the essential tools for the study of the Ancient Mediterranean world. The goal is for students to familiarize themselves with the methods, materials, and research resources of interdisciplinary Classics.

The course is required for Classics graduate students and should be taken as soon as possible after matriculation.

sections.title: Latin Literature Survey, Part II
sections.description: This course, taken in combination with Latin Literature Part I, offers a comprehensive survey of Latin literature from the Republican to the Imperial and Early Christian era. Students will read, translate, comment upon, and interpret selected passages to sharpen language skills and broader their understanding of major literary characteristics and trends.

sections.title: The Homeric Iliad
sections.description:
This course studies the Homeric Iliad. We will pay particular attention to features of the Homeric dialect and its meter and differences between reading epic in the modern sense and engaging in it as part of a performance culture. Participants will be expected to read the Iliad in its entirety in translation outside of class; course translation will focus on book 1 and then on the single day battle that occupies books 11–18. Discussions will survey different scholarly approaches to Homer, but will emphasize frameworks from performance studies, cognitive and affect theory, and insights from trauma studies. These different perspectives will support a deeper understanding of the interconnection between the structures of Homeric poetry and audience responses.

Knowledge of ancient Greek is required; but previous experience with Greek poetry is not. Students will be expected to read and discuss Greek texts in class.

sections.title: Ancient Medicine
sections.description: This course will explore a variety of textual and material evidence for health and healthcare in Greek and Roman antiquity. We will begin with a modern biography of Galen (who lived 129-ca.216 CE) to help situate us within Greco-Roman culture more broadly, as we prepare to delve into specific aspects of medical practice. Topics include the development of ‘scientific’ medicine alongside traditional beliefs that pointed to the gods as the cause of illness, the devastating social and physical effects of plague and other epidemics, theories and practices concerning female bodies, and alternatives to doctors such as temple healing and magic. Knowledge of ancient Greek, while helpful, is not required.

sections.title: The Art of Late Antique and Medieval Letters
sections.description:
This course introduces students to ancient, late antique, and early medieval letters and epistolography (the art of writing, circulating, and publishing letters). This course focuses on a single literary genre (letters) in a way that introduces students to wider research and reading methods relevant to premodern studies (ancient, late antique, medieval). Course readings will be in English; students with mastery of additional ancient/modern languages will be expected to incorporate these language skills in their research papers.

Extensive reading in Latin prose and poetry of the Augustan and imperial periods. Texts are studied in chronological sequence, and major themes of early imperial intellectual history are explored. Readings focus on literature of the golden and silver ages in a variety of genres, including epic, pastoral, tragic drama, satire, epigram, letters, and historical writings.

The development of Greek rhetoric and prose style. A review of morphology and syntax is followed by intensive close reading of selections from authors in chronological sequence. Emphasis is on close translation and syntactical and stylistic analysis.

This course will meet at 8 Washington ​Mews Room 105. This seminar introduces both the well-known and lesser-known Latin poets of Late Antiquity. We will examine the origins of Christian poetry (Commodian), the Christian Latin epic (Juvencus, Sedulius, Arator), the cento (Proba), and panegyric (Claudian, Sidonius Apollinaris, Corippus). We will read poets who engaged with and reshaped classical models (Prudentius, Dracontius, Pseudo-Prosper of Aquitaine, Boethius) and conclude with the prolific poets of Merovingian Gaul (Avitus of Vienne, Venantius Fortunatus). In addition, we will consider Christian theorizing about the correct purpose of literature, such as in Augustine’s De Doctrina Christiana and Paulinus of Nola’s rejection of his mentor Ausonius’s poetic model. While tracing the reception of classical poets, in particular Virgil and Ovid, we will also observe the parallel emergence of new formal developments such as the proliferation of accentual verse.

CLASS-GA 3002.001 Social Mobility in the Greek World, 800-50 B.C.

The social movement of people up and down the socioeconomic ladder is a phenomenon primarily associated with the modern, industrial world. Did it exist in the Greek Mediterranean? And what forms did it take in practice? What role did one’s legal status, sex, occupation, competence, and social networks, among other factors, play in shaping their opportunities, or lack thereof? To answer these questions, this seminar combines contemporary social science research on status, stratification, and inequality with close analysis of ancient evidence. Particular attention will be paid to epichoric differences (i.e., the ways individual city-states chose to regulate, promote, hinder, and react to social mobility), while the phenomenon itself will be studied over the longue durée. Our grounding in the Greek Mediterranean will provide ample opportunity for comparative work, and students will be exposed to different genres of evidence, including epic poetry, comedy, oratory, inscriptions, papyri, historiography, and ancient law and political thought.

This is an overview of the main developments in formal logic in Greek antiquity. Topics to be covered include: Aristotle’s theory of the categorical syllogism and its application in demonstrative science, Theophrastus' theory of the hypothetical syllogism, Stoic propositional logic, Galen’s account of relational syllogisms, and the reception of Peripatetic and Stoic logic in late antiquity, a comparison between ancient and modern logical theories. Our main text will be the earliest surviving handbook of logic in Greek, Galen’s Introduction to Logic (which we will read in the new edition with commentary by Barnes and Morison). NOTE: Department consent required. Please contact Jack Mikuszewski: jhm378@nyu.edu for permission to enroll in this course.

sections.title: Cervantes and Don Quixote: Reading, Rereading, Visualizing
sections.description: This course, which is taught in English and requires no reading knowledge of other languages, involves three aspects to be treated each week: first, a close collective reading of the whole text of Cervantes’s masterpiece; second, an analysis of the rereading of Don Quixote by later authors from Proust and Nabokov to Lukacs, Primo Levi, and García Márquez; and, finally, an introduction to the varied audiovisual versions of Cervantes’ original text, from different periods and countries. The course will graded by final paper (50%), midterm exam (25%), and final presentation, weekly postings to course website, and oral contribution to class (25%).​ The exam and final paper may be written in English or Spanish.

sections.title: Money and the Novel
sections.description:
It is a truth universally acknowledged” that the rise of the realist novel in the 18th and 19th centuries went hand in hand with a fixation on—to put it bluntly—money: that is, both socio-economic concerns such as class stratification, imperialism, the marriage market, and the ascent of capitalism, and as a material object as coins, paper money, credit, etc.. The New Economic Criticism has examined the fascinating relationships between literary narration and political economy, as well as the role money plays in the domestic sphere, particularly in 19th-century fiction. But what happens to the relationship between literary narration and economics in the transition from realism to modernism, which has received comparatively less scholarly attention?

In this course, we will explore the representation of money in a selection of English, American, and continental European novels and short fiction from roughly the 1720s to the 1930s. Readings will include fiction by realist authors such as Defoe, Burney, Austen, Balzac, Melville, and Zola alongside 20th-century works by Proust, Joyce, Woolf, Nella Larsen, Jean Rhys, Irmgard Keun, Anzia Yezierska, Dorothy Whipple, and others, plus key critical and theoretical texts including those by Marx, Simmel, Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Woolf again, Benjamin, Marc Shell, and John Vernon. We will examine how authors depict earning, spending, saving, and losing money, and how social and economic changes like poverty-driven immigration, war, stock market speculation, the Great Depression, and heightened consumerism shape the texts we read. Moreover, we will discuss whether and how money complicates traditional frameworks of periodization. While we will touch on how money can function metaphorically in fiction, our primary focus will be on material representations of what money is and what it does, and on how these representations relate to both social criticism and narrative style.

sections.title: Topics in Translation Studies
sections.description: This seminar explores the history and theory of translation in the West. We will read and discuss major theoretical texts that have shaped the field of translation studies from Cicero and St. Jerome to Luther, Schleiermacher, Goethe, Benjamin, Jakobson, Borges, Venuti, Derrida, Berman, Spivak, Kilito and Apter among others in order to work our way through the various aesthetic, ethical and political questions raised by the practice of translation. Alongside these theoretical essays, we will examine key translations of literary and other texts as case studies that test the limits of these theories. At the end of the term, each student willredact a discussion of a specific translation theory or set of theories, an analysis of a specific translation or an original translation accompanied by a critical introduction. The class will be taught in English, but participants should have working knowledge of at least one language other than English, preferably French, German or Spanish.

sections.title: The Novella as a Genre
sections.description: This course asks a simple question: what is a novella and how does it differ from a novel or a short story? This should not be a very difficult question. What is difficult is that given the instances of so many different novellas, it is necessary to understand how each redefines the genre. Is it even possible to ask what is a novella other than by its length? To ask a yet more pointed question: what is the kind of pleasure that a novella generates and how does it differ from what a novel has to offer?

sections.title: Neopolitan Narratives, from Elena Ferrante to Gomorrah: Literature, Cinema, Television
sections.description: Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan tetralogy shined a spotlight on an Italian city which had long exercised the imagination of philosophers, literati and visual artists. Called by Walter Benjamin a porous city for its theatrical architecture and for its ‘inexhaustible law of life’, Naples is not merely setting but protagonist in recent literary, cinematic, and televisual texts. Starting from the critical reflections of Benjamin, Antonio Gramsci and Franco Cassano, this course will discuss the complex portrayal of contemporary Naples in three different modules: the first and most extensive will center on Elena Ferrante’s entire literary production, while the second will analyze the cinematic works of a group of directors strongly associated to Naples: Mario Martone, Paolo Sorrentino, and Matteo Garrone. The seminar will conclude with a module that examines the representation of Naples in three series: the adaptations of Ferrante’s My Brilliant Friend and Roberto Saviano’s Gomorrah, and the breakout hit The Sea Outside. The course will be conducted in English.

sections.title: History of Literary Theory & Criticism II
sections.description: This course offers students an overview of the development and key elements of literary criticism from the late eighteenth century until the present day. We will begin with the study of Enlightenment and nineteenth-century discourses about literature. After that, we will examine various critical paradigms including psychoanalysis, structuralism, semiotics, deconstruction, feminism, and post-colonialism. We will look at the way these theories redefine our notions of aesthetics, politics, authority and authorship, subjectivity, textuality, historicity, and materialism. This course fulfills the second half of the requirement in History of Literary Theory for students in the Comparative Literature program.

sections.title: Critical Theory: Foundations and Practices
sections.description: Critical theory has never been a static collection of European texts. It is an active, urgent method for questioning the structures that shape our daily realities. Designed to fulfill the core requirement for the Critical Theory Certificate Program, this course introduces you to critical theory not as a historical artifact, but as a living toolkit for diagnosing the crises of the present. We will bridge the literary, sociological, psychological, and philosophical dimensions of the discipline to examine how power operates, how knowledge is produced, and how resistance is shaped in a globalized world. What makes this course distinct is our point of departure. We will read the foundational texts of the Frankfurt School and contemporary social theory through the lens of postcolonial territories. By shifting our geographic and intellectual center, we will explore how concepts of capitalism, modernity, culture, and state violence transform when viewed from the Global South. We will ask critical questions: How do colonial legacies persist in today's digital and economic systems? How do global inequalities manifest in local territories? And most importantly, what new forms of liberation and thought emerge from the margins? Together, we will fill the gap between abstract philosophy and concrete reality. This course is an invitation to unlearn dominant narratives, challenge the status quo, and re-envision the world from the very grounds we stand on. Through presentations and a final conference, you will be encouraged to directly apply and develop these theoretical frameworks within your own field of study.

Uneven Futures: Speculative Fictional Strategies for Collective Survival

Actors, Bodies, and Performance in Early Modern England
Interactive Data Visualization
sections.description: Interactive data visualization is one of the most engaging forms of communication today, helping users better understand complicated topics, detect patterns, and connect with powerful stories. This course explores what defines interactive data visualization, how interactive elements enhance comprehension, and why interactivity enables users to explore, analyze, and interpret complex data more effectively. Through hands-on labs, students will be introduced to a curated selection of modern web technologies including Observable and d3.js, and progress from foundational web development concepts to creating compelling interactive visualizations. By the end of the course, students will be able to articulate why interactivity is valuable, design and build interactive data visualizations tailored to different audiences and use cases, and have a working knowledge of key visualization frameworks. While no previous development experience is required, familiarity with visualization principles covered in DATA 73000 Visualization and Design, as well as basic HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, is helpful.

sections.title: Advanced Data Analysis
sections.description:
Note: Students should have a working knowledge of Statistics (through Regression methods) and at least a basic knowledge of Python to do the work required in this course. The course will be taught in Python, primarily using the scikit-learn library. Students should have completed DATA 71000 Data Analysis Methods or DATA 70500 Working with Data or have equivalent knowledge or experience. If questions about prior experience, or for permission, email the instructor.

This survey course is designed for students who want to extend their data analytic skills beyond a basic knowledge of multiple regression analysis, and who want to communicate their findings clearly to audiences of business groups, researchers, and other practitioners. The course will introduce students to advanced data analytic methods and toolkits, including machine learning methods using the scikit learning library, that will equip them with the ability to perform analyses of complex data from business, industry, and the arts and sciences. The course will begin with an overview of regression analyses, including logistic regression, and continues with latent variable analysis and related exploratory data analytic methods. This course will cover both supervised methods (e.g., k-Nearest neighbors, naïve Bayes classifiers, decision trees, and support vector machines) and unsupervised methods (e.g., principal component analysis, non-negative matrix factorization, and k-means clustering). The supervised methods will focus primarily on "classic" machine learning techniques where features are designed rather than learned, although we briefly look at recent deep learning models with neural networks The course will offer conceptual explanations of these statistical techniques and will provide opportunities for students to implement and practice these techniques using real data with the goal of helping students develop a sense of when machine learning is an appropriate tool versus other statistical modeling methods. Students will be encouraged to use Python and sci-kit learning tools to produce readable and sensible code that will enable others to replicate and extend their analyses.

sections.title: Software Design Lab: “Creative Computing”
sections.description:
Software Design Lab is an introduction to software development as a practice and creative medium through a hands-on approach.

This course will guide students in developing a coding craft that is grounded in iterative design and self-expression. This is a hands-on course that is light on theory: you will learn to code by gradually building their own interactive projects. You will explore how software can be used as a creative medium, and how it can be integrated into an existing research or artistic practice.

The course is run in a studio format, which means all students are expected to participate in the making, discussing, and critiquing work. Coursework will center around two web-based programming projects.

Prior coding experience is not required, and many students with no coding experience have succeeded in this course. However, if you are completely new to coding, expect a relatively steep learning curve in the 4-6 weeks of the course.

sections.title: Visualization and Design
sections.description: We live in a data-driven society where decisions are increasingly shaped by an analysis of “the data”, often communicated through visualizations. This course offers an introduction to the ever-evolving world of data visualization, beginning with its historical origins and culminating with a look toward the future of data viz and data-as-art. Through lectures, we will discuss the principles of good design and visual storytelling and practice how to understand, interpret, and communicate data for an audience effectively. Using Tableau as our primary tool, we will develop hands-on skills in cleaning, transforming, and connecting complex datasets, selecting appropriate chart types based on data structure and variable types, and constructing engaging narratives through visualization. Students will also engage in the iterative process of visualization through a series of 3 individual projects, and learn how to develop research questions, locate relevant datasets, interpret their findings, and exchange constructive feedback on their design choices. We will finish out the semester with a discussion of data as an artistic medium, examining how the visual language of art and design can critique and reimagine the role of data in society. Regardless of your academic concentration, you will walk away from this class with a portfolio of impressive visual analyses and a versatile, interdisciplinary skill set to apply in academic, professional, and creative pursuits

sections.title: Data, Culture and Society
sections.description:
Tuesday, 6:30 - 8:30 PM, 3 Credits, Prof. Katherine Behar (katherine.behar@baruch.cuny.edu)

Big data and computational methods for its analysis are changing scientific and humanities research, financial markets, political campaigning, higher education, and countless other areas, and also affect our everyday lives. Our daily existence is increasingly structured by software systems that process massive amounts of data and generate results such as music and book recommendations, search engine inputs, car routes, airline prices, etc.

In this course, we explore the social, political, and cultural impact of reliance of our society on massive (and often real-time) data analysis. We will discuss the concepts behind data collection, organization, analysis, and publication. We will also discuss possibilities, limitations, and implications of using big data-centric methods in social science and humanities research, and the already developed work in computational social science, digital humanities and cultural analytics fields. Students will become familiar with the history and basic concepts of the fundamental paradigms developed by modern societies to analyze patterns in data--statistics, visualization, data mining, and machine learning.

Finally, we also want to ask general questions about society and culture in a data-centric society. The arrival of social media and the gradual move of knowledge and media distribution and cultural communication to digital networks in the early 21st century has created a new digital landscape which challenges our existing methods for the study of and assumptions about culture. What new theoretical concepts do we need to deal with the new scale of born-digital culture? What data analysis and visualization techniques developed by industry and sciences are most useful for cultural analysis? How can we use big cultural data to question what we know about culture and generate new questions?

sections.title: Special Topics: "Computational Discourse Analysis with Python"
sections.description:
Note: Computational Discourse Analysis in Python satisfies as a Data Analysis distribution core course.

Note: Students should have at least a basic knowledge of statistical coding to do the required work for the course.

In this class, we'll examine computational methods for the analysis and visualization of large corpus text data. We'll begin with tools and techniques for building and managing a corpus (a collection of related documents), including scraping text from the web. Much of the analysis of text data involves modeling latent structure. We'll consider a variety of models, including conceptual network analysis, latent Dirichlet allocation, sentiment analysis, measures of similarity, and classification with machine learning.

sections.title: Special Topics: "Conflict Technology: Artificial Intelligence in Warfare and Surveillance”
sections.description:
Autonomous systems now direct weaponry, monitor borders, and police streets. This class will study these technologies and the technical, legal and ethical questions posed by their deployment internationally and domestically. Topics will include drone warfare, predictive policing, digital forensics, OSINT, evidence in domestic and international jurisprudence, and data ethics.

Centering the material artifacts and the data they train on, use, capture, store and transmit across complex interlocking networks and infrastructures, this class will:

attempt to uncover how they afford evidence for accountability and justice, for example in formal legal settings and open source investigations;

look at how theoretical and aesthetic responses to AI’s uses in conflict and control shape public policy and discourse.

The class will combine seminar style engagements with literature from surveillance studies, information studies, critical data studies, law, data science and adjacent fields, together with guest lectures, aesthetic forms of enquiry, and group research. Assessment will include a surveillance mapping project and analysis of an autonomous weapons system.

sections.title: Special Topics in Computational Fundamentals: "Scrollytelling with Civic Data"
sections.description:
Note: This is a 1-credit course. Students may take a maximum of three 1-credit courses (a total of 3 credits) for elective credits.

It’s a snowstorm out there, and the road is more obscured than ever. We are confronted with so much data that ten lifetimes hardly seems enough to parse through it. In the face of this, effective data analysis communication to broad audiences calls for numeric findings to be delivered in a selective, clear and memorable sequence–or narrative.

This lab class will focus on using Closeread, an extension for the Quarto publishing platform that converts scripted data analysis into a scrollable, multi-step web page that delivers insights at the user’s own pace. Students will develop their own “scrollytelling” projects using data from the NYC Open Data repository or other publicly available data source, and present their findings in person at a dedicated showcase as part of NYC Open Data Week in April. Some coding experience is desirable, though not essential as long as the student is willing to take on a steep learning curve. The class will be taught in R, using RStudio, but students are also welcome to develop their project using Python, Julia or ObservableJS.

sections.description:
Wednesday, 11:45 AM - 1:45 PM, 3 Credits, Prof. Katie Cumiskey (katie.cumiskey@csi.cuny.edu)

“AI for What?! A Public Interest Technology Studio” is a project-based graduate course developed through the CUNY Public Interest Technology Lab (CUNY PIT Lab). Students work with city agencies, community organizations, and mission-driven partners on real-world challenges involving digital tools, data, design, media, emerging technologies, and AI.

Projects begin with relationships, community needs, and public problems, not with the assumption that technology is the answer. Through fieldwork, participatory research, human-centered design, evaluation, and collaborative problem-solving, students build practical skills while engaging questions of equity, accessibility, privacy, accountability, and community voice. Digital equity, diverse futurisms, and approaches to reclaiming technology for the public good guide the studio.

Students should expect about six hours per week outside class, consistent with Graduate Center expectations for a three-credit course, including partner meetings, site visits, collaboration, research, and project development.

The semester culminates in a co-created, co-owned, portfolio-ready project designed for real-world use.

sections.title: Digital Humanities: Methods and Practices
sections.description:
Note: DH Methods and Practices is a required core course in the MA in DH Program.

During the Fall 2026 semester, students explored the landscape of the digital humanities, considering a range of approaches to scholarship in the field and developing proposals for potential projects. In the spring, we will put that thinking into action by working collaboratively to refine and develop a small number of those proposals into working prototypes.

In this praxis-oriented course, students will gain hands-on experience in conceptualizing, planning, building, and disseminating DH projects. Working in teams, they will develop and apply technical, project management, and communication skills as they navigate the practical and intellectual challenges of collaborative DH work, including the opportunities and perils that generative AI presents for the field.

One of our goals is to produce well-conceived, sustainable projects that have the potential to grow beyond the Spring 2027 semester. A range of advisors may be matched to support the needs of each individual project. Successful completion of the course will require a commitment to collaborative work and to meeting mutually agreed-upon milestones and deadlines established at the beginning of the semester. The course will culminate in a public showcase where students will launch their project prototypes and receive feedback from the GC digital humanities community.
