sections.title: Earth Systems II
sections.description:
Enrollment: Course open to EES students only. Other programs register with Instructor Permission. [Required EGS].

The objectives of this semester of the Earth Systems sequence are to 1) continue to develop a strong foundational understanding of Earth’s systems, with a focus on the fundamental concepts governing Earth’s hydrosphere and the biosphere, to 2) understand the dynamic interconnected between Earth’s spheres and their processes (geosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, biosphere), 3) understand the interplay between natural variability and human activities, the effects of these activities on Earth’s systems, and practices to offset negative effects.

sections.title: Topics in Environmental Psychology
sections.description:
Enrollment: Course open to EES students only. Other programs register with Instructor Permission. [Required EP].

This seminar explores various topics within the multidisciplinary field of Environmental Psychology ranging from research, practice, pedagogy, and current issues. The format includes presentations and discussions by guests, faculty, alumni, and current students.

sections.title: Current Issues in EES
sections.description:
Enrollment: Course open to EES Students only. [Required for 1st year Geog., EP., EGS].

Weekly colloquium series featuring speakers from the EES Program and visitors from other academic departments and organizations throughout NYC, the United States, and beyond. The series alternates between presentations from Geographers and Earth and Geological Scientists and aims to showcase current research and critical issues. Occasionally a colloquium session is dedicated to student professional development panels and student presentations. An EES student is responsible for introducing the visiting speaker each week. Lively discussion is always encouraged.

sections.title: EGS [55721] Qualifying Paper Workshop
sections.description: This workshop provides structured guidance and peer support for writing your advisor-supervised qualifying paper - a key component of the EGS qualifying exam procedure. Beyond a comprehensive literature review grounding your work in the discipline, the paper asks you to begin to articulate your research agenda, outline probable methodologies, and envision your contributions to the field. Working closely with your advisor and later another EGS faculty readers helps build key academic relationships, while asynchronous discussion forums and optional weekly Zoom “live hour” offer peer feedback and collaboration throughout the writing process. Reach out for a syllabus.

sections.title: Geographic Thought and Theory II
sections.description:
Enrollment: Course open to EES students only. Other programs register with Instructor Permission. [Required for 1st year Geography]

This course delves more deeply into the debates, concepts, theories, and methodologies in human geography covered in Geographic Thought and Theory I. A primary objective of this course is to equip students with the theoretical and methodological tools necessary to undertake their own research projects. The course is reading-intensive, with a focus on seminal works (monographs) written by CUNY Graduate Center geographers, as well as by other critical human geographers writing across a range of topics and adopting a variety of theoretical and methodological approaches. Requirements include attendance and participation, leading class discussion, a book review, and a seminar paper.

sections.title: Research Design and Methodologies
sections.description: This seminar is designed to introduce and develop a working knowledge of research design and methods for geography and other social sciences. It is a semester long course that will require 1) reading, 2) written reports, 3) leading a class discussion, and 4) fieldwork on a site in New York City where you will be able to try out each method. The emphasis is on learning through reading and lectures as well as through application, practice and class critique. Classes will run as both a graduate seminar with intellectual content and as a methods workshop.

sections.title: Geographies of Peace and Conflict
sections.description: While geography historically served the mechanics of war and empire, recent decades have seen scholars establish peace as an essential geographic concept, keyword, and site of critical inquiry. This PhD seminar interrogates the complex challenges to peace amidst contemporary, cascading, and systemic crises. Through a close reading of core geographic frameworks and spatial methodologies, we will examine the conceptual and analytical friction and alignments between peace geographies, abolition geographies, and the broader “spatial turn” in peace and conflict studies. Students will actively engage with current debates, field-based research, and emerging topics related to peace and conflict, with the seminar serving as a collaborative forum to chart the future horizons and possibilities of peace geographies.

sections.title: Solidarity Cities
sections.description:
Enrollment: Course open to all GC students.

The new course “Solidarity Cities” will examine how people in the U.S. and around the world have been building cities (and beyond) based on solidarity rather than profit and competition. In doing so, they have collectively shaped urban spaces according to their needs and dreams. Is the production of solidarity-based urban space and related struggles a marginal utopian project? Or is it a widespread yet invisible practice rooted in social reproduction, livelihoods, and mutual aid? Although racial capitalism and neoliberal forces appear to have fully defined our cities, people have long drawn on various forms of solidarity (economic, social, cultural, and political) to remake urban areas—despite all barriers—into cities of collective resistance to harm, cities of collective consumption and public goods, and cities of cooperation and mutual aid.

sections.title: Political Ecology of Social and Environmental Justice
sections.description:
This seminar examines classic and contemporary works on how social and environmental injustice is produced, understood, and resisted. It offers a broad overview of social theory relevant to the study of people-environment relations, tracing connections to contemporary environmental and climate justice scholarship and activism. Using a political ecology framework, we will pay attention to how the unequal distribution of environmental harms and benefits is produced at various scales and in locations across the globe, with a focus on how individuals and communities experience, understand, and respond to environmental degradation and climate change.

We will consider a range of practices and theoretical understandings from north and south to explore ethical, methodological, and epistemological debates in political ecology, as well as political ecological factors (including spatial, cultural, technological, and psychological factors) that enable and constrain the just futures that scholars, activists, and communities imagine, as they reconfigure relations to nature, cities, the earth, and themselves through their struggles for social, epistemic, environmental, and climate justice.

sections.title: Social Reproduction
sections.description: Social reproduction is a geographically and historically differentiated process encompassing the production of a stratified labor force and the cultural forms and practices that create and maintain its differences while making them common sense. It involves both the sensuous labor of everyday life and the structured practices that unfold in dialectical relation to production. These material social practices take place across geographic and temporal scales, encompassing daily and generational relations that are as much intimate as global in their effects and charge. Social reproduction also involves the reproduction of the material grounds and conditions of production, including the conservation of environmental resources and the concerns of environmental justice. The work of social reproduction is racialized, gendered and class specific, and is accomplished within a contested and shifting amalgam that includes the family, household, state, workplace, and institutions of civil society. The critical inquiry of these concerns and the materials social practices associated with social reproduction will be our focus in this seminar.

sections.title: Environmental Justice Policies and Practices
sections.description: This course focuses on the distributional dimensions of environmental degradation and environmental protection globally, domestically and in New York City. We will explore the social processes that generate synergistic race and class stratification, and how they impact the distribution of ecological costs and benefits. Substantive areas of focus will include the class and racial segregation of urban neighborhoods, the siting of hazardous facilities in communities of color, unequal protection of environmental health, unequal distribution of urban environmental amenities, and climate injustice. The course will also examine the social origins and impacts of a distinct environmental justice movement that emerged from BIPOC and working-class communities that are most at risk from climate change. Both successes and ongoing struggles in the EJ movement will be explored, with emphasis on NYC.

sections.title: Seminar in Special Topics: AI for What?! A Public Interest Technology Studio
sections.description: This studio-style course brings students and mission-driven organizations together as equal collaborators to co-create critical AI practices and approaches to emerging technologies. Each week, organizational partners join the class to share real-world contexts and engage in dialogue and design. A critical narrative of tech integration will center equity, transparency, and community voice. Field placements extend this collaboration as mixed teams conduct needs assessments and develop implementation strategies focused on shaping social outcomes and organizational effectiveness and efficiencies. The semester culminates in a jointly authored, portfolio-ready deliverable grounded in community priorities and critical AI practice.

sections.title: Uneven Futures: Speculative Fictional Strategies for Collective Survival
sections.description:
Science fiction author William Gibson once remarked that the future is already here – it just isn’t evenly distributed. It doesn’t take much to extrapolate Gibson’s comment about the unequally distribution of futurity to a global geographical plane characterized by intensifying combined and uneven development. But are the core capitalist countries – the so-called West – still the domicile of futurity? How might the implied temporal, spatial, and developmental hierarchies in Gibson’s quip by inverted? How can temporality be decolonized, and what role can fiction play in this effort to imagine alternative radical futures?

This seminar examines works of speculative fiction that engage in what Kodwo Eshun argues is the “chronopolitical act” of intervening in the production and distribution of futurity. To dismantle Western narratives of progress and modernity that are premised on the historical subjugation of people of color is also to confound the Western dichotomy between the real and unreal, the scientific and the supernatural. The seminar will, therefore, be filled with spirits, ghosts, and ancestral intelligence (AI) that circulates in the present and imparts lessons about the future. There will also, of course, be lots of cyborgs. We will attend to the long legacy of genres like Afrofuturism while also investigating Africanfuturism and speculative fictions set in other parts of the Global South. Of key interest will be recent works of postcolonial cli-fi that attempt to think through strategies of collective survival in the face of the climate emergency, which is unfolding with greatest ferocity in the Global South. Foundational to all our discussions will be investigation of the way in which aesthetic genres warp, morph, and are reborn under the pressure of the quest to forge new futures.

Some of the authors and critics whose work we are likely to discuss include Octavia Butler, T.J. Demos, Cherie Dimaline, Amal El-Mohtar, Kodwo Eshun, Mark Fisher, Amitav Ghosh, Megha Majumdar, Masande Ntshanga, M.E. O’Brien and Eman Abdelhadi, Nnedi Okorafor, Rebecca Roanhorse, Rosaura Sánchez and Beatrice Pita, Boualem Sansal, Tade Thompson!

sections.title: The US Imperial Crisis and the Horizons of Emancipation
sections.description:
Enrollment: Course open to EES students only. Instructor permission required. Students should email one paragraph explaining how the course fits into their studies to Jeffmaskovsky@gc.cuny.edu

What kind of critical work on the United States should scholars produce to defend precarious lives amidst an ongoing US imperial crisis? How might we advance political stances that illuminate the horizons of emancipation and contribute to the end of oppression, violence, and exploitation in all their forms? This course seeks to address these questions by foregrounding recent contributions from American studies, Black diasporic studies, critical ethnic studies, Native studies, literary studies, anthropology, and history on the relations of capitalism and colonialism through which the United States is produced and reproduced as a concrete social formation. Working to unsettle the methodological nationalism and American exceptionalism that are hallmarks of conventional American accounts, we seek instead to reconsider "the United States" by treating it as a problematic, contradiction-laden space concealing global operations of colonial and imperial power. Extending the interventions by scholars working on racial capitalism, the Atlantic and Pacific worlds, gendered racial terror, settler colonialism, the violence of liberal humanism, and related reassessment and reorientation concerning liberalism, humanity, land, enclosure, containment, labor, property, territory, empire, dispossession, freedom, sovereignty, modernity, and other key words, we will work together to uncover the death-dealing logics and practices that define the contemporary imperial crisis. And we will explore the substance and limits of abolitionist and other counter-hegemonic political projects, asking what they demand of us as engaged scholars and how their emancipatory horizons must change to address the shifting dynamics of imperial decline.

sections.title: Figures of Anti-Imperialism: Palestine, Islam, Marxism
sections.description:
This course begins from the national liberation movements that oppose U.S. imperialism today, both in Palestine and around it. The premise of the course is that we won’t appreciate the logic of these movements until we understand what is specific to the imperial formation they oppose and, by extension, its difference from prevailing concepts of empire. To that end, we will consider Marxist theories of imperialism, homing in especially on the presumption—contested by Third-World Marxists (e.g., Mariátegui, Mao, Fanon, Che, Cabral, Amin)—that the industrial working classes must become the revolutionary subjects of history (e.g., Lenin, Trotsky, Gramsci, Luxemburg, Lukács). We will study, pace that presumption, the implication in recent scholarship that US empire depends less on colonized labor than on ‘accumulation by waste’ (Ali Kadri, Michael Denning, Ruth Wilson Gilmore). Such scholarship details how the dominant forms of capital (i.e., military industrial, technology and surveillance, finance) profit from surplus and disposable populations by testing the technology of genocide on them (Zygmunt Bauman, William Robinson). In both Palestine and the broader region, we will study the history by which Marxist liberation movements were largely replaced by Islamic ones and consider how the tactics, politics, and metaphysics of both these phases of anti-imperial struggle respond to the mode of accumulation they confront. We might read Ghassan Kanafani, Arwa Saleh, or Mahdi Amel on the Marxist side and Sayyid Qutb, Zaynab Al-Ghazali, Malcolm X, or Ali Shariati on the Islamic side.

As it explores these theoretical contexts, the course will have two other tasks. We will examine the adequacy of received anti-imperial scholarship (e.g., Jameson, Said, Spivak, Davis, Butler, Mbembe, Khalidi, Kelley, Moten, Coulthard) to the material actualities of empire and reflect on this scholarship’s curious reticence toward the revolutionary movements fighting empire now. And we will study how, in thinking with such movements, literature from Palestine and the region expands the field of Western aesthetic perception and how it does not (e.g., Tayeb Salih, Emile Habibi, Kanafani, Sahar Khalifeh, Radwa Ashour, Susan Abulhawa, Wisam Rafeedie).

Prior knowledge of these topics is neither expected nor desired. The point of the course is to build understanding from the ground up. Despite the breadth of topics, weekly readings will be selective and manageable.

sections.title: Uneven Futures: Speculative Fictional Strategies for Collective Survival
sections.description:
Science fiction author William Gibson once remarked that the future is already here – it just isn’t evenly distributed. It doesn’t take much to extrapolate Gibson’s comment about the unequally distribution of futurity to a global geographical plane characterized by intensifying combined and uneven development. But are the core capitalist countries – the so-called West – still the domicile of futurity? How might the implied temporal, spatial, and developmental hierarchies in Gibson’s quip by inverted? How can temporality be decolonized, and what role can fiction play in this effort to imagine alternative radical futures?

This seminar examines works of speculative fiction that engage in what Kodwo Eshun argues is the “chronopolitical act” of intervening in the production and distribution of futurity. To dismantle Western narratives of progress and modernity that are premised on the historical subjugation of people of color is also to confound the Western dichotomy between the real and unreal, the scientific and the supernatural. The seminar will, therefore, be filled with spirits, ghosts, and ancestral intelligence (AI) that circulates in the present and imparts lessons about the future. There will also, of course, be lots of cyborgs. We will attend to the long legacy of genres like Afrofuturism while also investigating Africanfuturism and speculative fictions set in other parts of the Global South. Of key interest will be recent works of postcolonial cli-fi that attempt to think through strategies of collective survival in the face of the climate emergency, which is unfolding with greatest ferocity in the Global South. Foundational to all our discussions will be investigation of the way in which aesthetic genres warp, morph, and are reborn under the pressure of the quest to forge new futures.

Some of the authors and critics whose work we are likely to discuss include Octavia Butler, T.J. Demos, Cherie Dimaline, Amal El-Mohtar, Kodwo Eshun, Mark Fisher, Amitav Ghosh, Megha Majumdar, Masande Ntshanga, M.E. O’Brien and Eman Abdelhadi, Nnedi Okorafor, Rebecca Roanhorse, Rosaura Sánchez and Beatrice Pita, Boualem Sansal, Tade Thompson!

sections.title: Critical Disability Studies
sections.description: Disability studies is an emerging, flourishing field, an exciting new way of thinking about bodyminds in the world. This course aims to give students a strong grounding in the fundamental principles and foundational texts of disability studies, including writings on the normate by Lennard Davis and Rosemarie Garland Thomson, core readings by Christine Miserandino and Tobin Siebers, along with care ethics by Eva Feder Kittay and Nel Noddings. We’ll build on this to address the theoretical interests that dominate the field today, including crip time, disability-gain, neurodiversity, queer-crip alignments, disability and race, accommodation theory, reading writers including Alison Kafer, H. Dirksen-Baumann, Margaret Price, Eli Clare, Leah Lakshmi Piepzna-Samrasinha, Elizabeth Freeman, Sami Schalk. One of the issues we’ll be thinking about is the extent to which academia reinforces a narrow sense of acceptable bodyminds, and how we might creatively expand that in our own work, including our teaching. Another key component of this course will be a deep dive into the historical construction of disability, with particular attention to the way alternative understandings of disability in the past might provide useful templates for us today (readings may include Susan Schweik, Paul Longmore, Jay Dolmage, Sarah Rose, Essaka Joshua, Michael Brown, and others). Because the modern idea of disability emerged in the nineteenth century, three short case studies will help us notice when it coheres and when it remains surprisingly fluid: Austen’s Mansfield Park, Dickens’s A Christmas Carol, and Oliphant’s The Library Window. Students will be encouraged to explore minds and bodies in the texts or cultural issues they care about most. The course will accommodate multiple forms of accountability in different media: weekly summaries, presentations, nontraditional or traditional final papers. I am excited to share this revelatory, reparative, expansive theoretical attunement with students, and to see what you make of it in your own fields.

sections.title: Barthes/Foucault/Kristeva: Texts as a Revolution
sections.description:
This course will focus on three of the most salient participants in the fecund intellectual cauldron of Paris during the 1960s and 1970s: Roland Barthes, Michel Foucault, and Julia Kristeva. They were, respectively, a philologist, a philosopher, and a psychoanalyst by training, but in an intellectual moment that was beginning to fumble beyond existentialism and structuralism toward a better understanding of an increasingly globalist world, these three scholars’ works overlapped and sometimes directly commented on each other. For us in the twenty-first century, postmodernism is a ground-level assumption about the world in which we live, but for these three thinkers “postmodernism” was a “discovery”—in precisely the same way that many before them might have said that Christopher Columbus “discovered” “America.” To put it baldly, they saw things that already existed and gave them newly recognizable names. In terms that Foucault would eventually coin, they identified a moment of epistemological emergence.

In this course, we will read works by all three scholars in the order in which they were originally published, in an attempt to track the exact movements in their thought through which that thought emerged. With the inevitable skeptical wisdom of hindsight, we will also question whether any of their intellectual movements might in retrospect appear to have been wrong turnings. Among the works that we may read in common are: Writing Degree Zero, Mythologies, A History of Madness, The Order of Things, and Discipline and Punish, as well as essays in both Image/Music/Text and The Kristeva Reader. We will pay central attention to three groundbreaking works that were published within a year of each other—S/Z, The Archeology of Knowledge, and Desire in Language—all of which arrived in the immediate wake of 1968, a year of very palpable revolutionary barricades on the streets of Paris just outside these three scholars’ classrooms and studies. We will also probably read A Lover’s Discourse, The History of Sexuality, and Tales of Love against one another, as well as Barthes’ and Kristeva’s self-conscious engagements with exoticism in Empire of Signs and About Chinese Women.

sections.title: Romantic Concepts of Nature
sections.description:
Since the rise of ecocriticism and Green Romanticism in the 1990s it has become commonplace to present Romantic writers as anticipating contemporary environmental concerns and to (re)mobilize for current ecological debates the Romantic critique of nascent processes of industrialization and a Cartesian, mechanical, view of the natural world. At the same time, ecologists and environmental writers perceive the “romanticization” of nature—the projection of imaginary, aesthetic and cultural constructs onto a material world fundamentally alien to them—as one of the main obstacles to a fruitful understanding of our relationship to the environment. More recently, ecocritics and ecopoets have come to suggest that, given the unraveling of the nature/culture binary and any stable conception of “Nature” in the disastrous predicament of our Anthropocene present, investigations of Romantic-era literature and culture are no longer applicable to the urgent needs of the present moment. Hence, in the contemporary discussion, one can see the Romantics being lauded for writing against the objectification of nature, being critiqued for neglecting the difference between the products of the writer’s consciousness and affect and the material Other they confront, and being dismissed as irrelevant for current ecological thought.

To position ourselves with respect to such conflicting assessments, we will investigate what a variety of Romantic-period concepts of nature—a plurality rather than a single position—looked like concretely. We will examine two of the central philosophical positions on the relationship of human consciousness to the natural world Romantic-era writers could draw on, those of Baruch Spinoza and Immanuel Kant, and discuss the writings and philosophical positions of Mary Wollstonecraft, William and Dorothy Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and John Clare. Throughout, our goal will be to ascertain the answers the texts of these writers can offer to questions about the place of human beings in the natural world, the relationship of mind and matter, and of human and natural history, central philosophical questions they indeed share with contemporary environmental thinkers.

sections.title: American Renaissance
sections.description: The American Renaissance (1835-65) is widely seen as the peak of American cultural expression. This period featured landmark writings race and slavery by Frederick Douglass, Harriet Jacobs, and Harriet Beecher Stowe; innovations in philosophy, ecological awareness, and style by Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau; the metaphysical depth and cultural variety exhibited through the fiction of Herman Melville and Nathaniel Hawthorne; the poetic experiments of Walt Whitman and Emily Dickinson; and the psychological exploration and groundbreaking aesthetics of Edgar Allan Poe. Women’s rights were forcibly promoted by Margaret Fuller and other feminists. Abolitionist activism ranged from the rhetorical militancy of William Lloyd Garrison to the armed action of John Brown. Lincoln’s speeches embodied the nation’s enduring political themes. This era also saw a surge in popular culture, exemplified by penny newspapers, pulp novels, graphic reform writings, and nation-touring singing families. Alongside studying key works of the period, we examine current approaches to cultural history, American Studies, and the study of race and gender. The course also investigates how online archives and AI can help us gain new insights that lead to original scholarship and potentially publishable writing.

sections.title: Improvisation
sections.description:
From Yvonne Rainer’s autobiography: “Ruth Barnes, who studied with me between 1969 and 1971, recently described the first dance class she attended in my studio on Greene Street: ‘When I came in, Yvonne was lying on the floor. When everyone was assembled she went into a closet and came out with a huge garbage bag, which she emptied. After fifty green tennis balls [I remember them as red rubber balls!] tumbled out, she said, ‘Get to work.’ And that was the class. I’ve never seen adults so intensely involved in such serious uncompetitive play.”

In this seminar, we will think and write together about how to improvise and about why one might be motivated to embark upon an improvisatory practice, whether in words, music, movement, or images. Key texts will be Fred Moten’s In the Break: The Aesthetics of the Black Radical Tradition, Yvonne Rainer’s Feelings Are Facts: A Life, Jack Whitten’s Notes from the Woodshed, John Cage’s Silence, Bernadette Mayer’s Midwinter Day, and Gertrude Stein’s A Novel of Thank You. We may also read selections from Ann Cooper Albright and David Gere’s Taken by Surprise: A Dance Improvisation Reader, Danielle Goldman’s I Want to be Ready: Improvised Dance as a Practice of Freedom, Derek Bailey’s Improvisation: Its Nature and Practice in Music, George Lewis’s A Power Stronger Than Itself: The AACM and American Experimental Music, as well as John Cassavetes’s Opening Night (starring Gena Rowlands), and texts and interviews by Pauline Oliveros, Park McArthur, Will Rawls, David Antin, and others.

sections.title: Heated Chivalry: Romance, Medieval and Beyond
sections.description:
This course will consider the genre of romance, from its earliest medieval instantiations through contemporary popular romances like Heated Rivalry.

The first two-thirds of the course will focus on medieval romance, examining intensively a series of (mostly poetic) texts, stretching from the romances and lais of Chretien de Troyes and Marie de France (in the 12th century) to Thomas Malory’s Morte Darthur (in the 15th). Along the way, we will consider romances about Charlemagne, Alexander, the Crusades, Arthur, the Grail, ancient Greece and Rome, “modern” England and France. Although we begin with texts written in French, we will treat mainly English-language texts, and we will read these in the original Middle English.

In the next third of the course, we will consider where romance travels after the 15th century. The syllabus here will partly depend upon student interest. (So, if we have a number of early modern students or Americanists, we will focus attention toward their fields of expertise.) We might read Philip Sidney or Mary Wroth; Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale; Sir Walter Scott or Nathaniel Hawthorne; Virginia Woolf’s Orlando, with an eye toward considering how these take up the mantle of the earlier romance genre while transforming it. And we will end by thinking about (queer?) romance in our current moment through the lens of Heated Rivalry—considering (again, partly based on students’ interests) either (or both) of Rachel Reid’s novels, Heated Rivalry and The Long Game, the Jacob Tierney television series, and some of the now voluminous fan fiction.

One central goal of the course will be to reflect on what we mean by the genre of romance, and to consider how we might approach the question of genre theoretically. Alongside the romance texts, we will therefore take up a wide range of approaches to theorizing genre: formalist arguments like Todorov’s; feminist readings like Radway’s; reception theory like Jauss’s; Marxist/materialist formulations like Lukács’s and Jameson’s; cultural studies projects like Modleski’s.

For non-medievalists, projects on later cultural materials are encouraged. For medievalists, interdisciplinary approaches (e.g., thinking about Crusades-related romances in relation to the historiography of the Crusades; considering works across different linguistic/national traditions; thinking comparatively about the representation of something like “courtly love” or “chivalry” in both literary works and non-literary modes like the visual arts) are welcome.

sections.title: Cinema of the Apocalypse
sections.description: Obviously, while the recent global pandemic has spurred new interest in the genre of viral calamity--films like Outbreak, Contagion, 28 Days (Years) Later, etc--the subject and sense of apocalypse has been integral to the history of cinema itself, as if its apparatus and ways of seeing open up the art before the otherwise inscrutable and abstract concepts of doom and end of days. To some extent this can be measured in the formal compulsions of visual narrative, and it is for this reason that film is often interpellated to address the immediacy and affective intimacy of catastrophe (an apocalypse “nowness” if you will). This course is intended to examine both the genealogies of representing apocalypse in film, a longue durée, say, from Verdens Undergang (1916) to Don’t Look Up (2021), but also to explore the situatedness of individual narratives that struggle to express both the desire and disavowal of imagining the end of the species and that of the world. With the sensitive dependence to historical conditions, for instance, Cold War catastrophe could be linked to anxiety about nuclear destruction (films like Fail-Safe [1964] or Dr. Strangelove [1964]) or sci-fi doppelgangers around Soviet invasion (The Thing from Another World [1951], The Day the Earth Stood Still [1951], Them! [1954]). We will look to complicate the conditions of spectatorship between, for instance, The Night of the Living Dead (1968), the perhaps radiation-tainted reanimation of “ghouls” and zombies, and Zombieland: Double Tap (2019), where even the banalization of annihilation is banalized. Indeed, the latter connects to a whole sub-genre of laughing in the face of the cannibalistic undead (Shaun of the Dead [2004]) or murderous aliens, (Mars Attacks! [1996], Attack the Block [2011]). The demise of the human is often imagined as a consequence of overpopulation or the end of reproduction, from Soylent Green (1973) and Avengers: Infinity War (2018) to Children of Men (2006), Mad Max: Fury Road (2015) and The Girl with All the Gifts (2016). Here we will consider why apocalypse is often linked to normative assumptions about gender and sexuality and the transformations of social reproduction as such. The racialization of future dread is also a significant focus of cinema, and where racial anxiety is both exposed and critiqued (Alien Nation [1988], District 9 [2009], Us [2019]. Indeed, apocalypse as a theme can be used to cross-reference and interrogate the codes of conscious and unconscious identification and alienation throughout the genre. Apocalypse from this perspective might offer discourses of a great leveling, and yet it is just as clear that film attempts to negotiate the gnawing persistence of inequalities on a world scale (the reproduction of class hierarchy in, for instance, Elysium [2013] and Snowpiercer [2013]). While cinematic apocalypse is never an unalloyed barometer of social anxiety, the effulgence of films of environmental catastrophe is significant in its own right. Often such narratives offer an imaginary resolution of a real contradiction: The Day after Tomorrow (2004), for instance, seems to place its bets on a father and son reuniting, while The Wandering Earth (2019) envisages the entire planet being dragged to safety. This suggests that fighting for change may not have the visual allure of suffering the consequences of quiescence. Nevertheless, in general the cinema of the apocalypse is the scene of conflicted allegories over and above the sublation of causes and effects, and the readings for the course will move between theory and fiction to elaborate this tension (a list might include Cameron, Chaudhary, Gurr, Knight, Kristeva, Martin et al, McCarthy, Butler, Missari, Seed, Sharrett, Shaviro, Sontag, Stone, Subramanian, and Vandemeer).

sections.title: Late Medieval and Early Modern Theatre and Performance
sections.description:
(Cross-listed with Theater – THEA 86000; Global Early Modern Studies Certificate Program – GEMS 83100)

This course offers an interdisciplinary introduction to theatre and performance in England and Europe from the 1400s through 1600s. Combining historical and theoretical approaches from a variety of disciplines, we will examine a range of dramatic genres, such as biblical theatre, saints plays, moralities, farces, revenge tragedy, commedia dell’arte, and court masques. We will also consider performance practices that were unscripted, improvised, or spectacular in nature, such as clowning, jigs, ballads, puppetry, rope-dancing, mountebank shows, bearbaiting, morris dancing, and civic pageantry. These various kinds of theatre and performance will be situated in relation to broader cultural discourses from the era, including those related to gender, sexuality, class, race, and religion, among others.

In addition to historicist concerns, we will also address theoretical and methodological matters, including both practical strategies for dealing with primary sources from this period and analytical reflection on epistemological questions raised by their idiosyncratic forms. Discussion may encompass the portability of critical tools developed to grapple with obsolete performance genres, unfamiliar documentary conventions, fragmentary sources, and gaps in evidence. In doing so, the course aims to invite a reevaluation of paradigms taken for granted in contemporary theatre research as well as self-reflexive examination of the theoretical stakes of that work.

Primary readings will include both dramatic literature and other extant texts related to performance, such as inventories of costumes and props. Secondary readings will be drawn from a variety of fields, including theatre and performance, cultural history, literature, art history, and religious studies. Non-English material will be provided in translation. No experience with paleography is required. Evaluation: active class participation, short weekly response papers, in-class presentation, research proposal with annotated bibliography, and a final paper.

sections.title: Actors, Bodies, and Performance in Early Modern England
sections.description: This course will explore ways that actors, both individually and collectively, shaped the construction of plays in early modern England. How did the members and power dynamics of repertory companies inspire playwrights’ development of characters and plots? What can we learn from accounts of actors in plays and other documents, and how did recognizable bodies interact with prosthetics such as wigs, cosmetics, blackface, and physical deformities? How might factors such as height, build, beards, voices, previous acting parts, and reputations have affected roles, and how did authors and audiences play with conventional practices of crossing lines of gender, race, class, and age? How did economics and company status affect casting and roles?

sections.title: The Art of Late Antique and Medieval Letters
sections.description:
(Cross-listed with Classics – CLAS 72800; Medieval Studies Certificate Program - MSCP 70100; Liberal Studies - MALS 74400)

This course introduces students to ancient, late antique, and early medieval letters and epistolography (the art of writing, circulating, and publishing letters). This course focuses on a single literary genre (letters) in a way that introduces students to wider research and reading methods relevant to premodern studies (ancient, late antique, medieval). Course readings will be in English; students with mastery of additional ancient/modern languages will be expected to incorporate these language skills in their research papers.

sections.title: Afropsychedelic: Black Experimental Forms in the 1970s
sections.description: What would it mean to know the world without repeating the structures that make antiblackness thinkable? This seminar works through Afropsychedelic, a framework for reading Black experimental forms as a practice of freedom that breaks open perception, narrative time, and genre so Black freedom dreams become imaginable on their own terms. We will read, among others, Carlene Hatcher Polite’s obscure novel Sister X and the Victims of Foul Play (1975), Toni Cade Bambara’s anthology The Black Woman (1970), poetry and manifestos from the Black Aesthetic Movement, and Melvin Van Peebles’s film Sweet Sweetback’s Baadasssss Song (1971). We will also consider the Caribbean Artists Movement, founded in London in 1966, where C. L. R. James joined early debates, and to its journal Savacou, launched in Jamaica in 1970, where Sylvia Wynter published “Novel and History, Plot and Plantation” (1971). Alongside Wynter and James, Margo Crawford, Carter Mathes, Nathaniel Mackey, Phillip Brian Harper, Carole Boyce Davies, and Jayna Brown will help us think about the human, abstraction, and other ways of knowing.

sections.title: Negative Aesthetics in U.S. Latinx Literatures
sections.description: For the last two centuries, Latinx authors in the U.S. have forged a literary tradition predicated on complex rearticulations of American sensibilities through generative forms of negativity. In this course we will consider, using Adorno as a theoretical springboard, how Latinx writers employ the negative to split and recombine languages, creolize racial identities, reimagine borders, and queer exile; and in so doing alter our notion of what constitutes aesthetic production, experience, and judgment. This literary sensibility runs counter, for instance, to Whitmanian flourishes of optimism or the ideological insistence on positivity that often veils the violence of colonial and market practices. Thus, we will examine how the formation of U.S. Latinx literary aesthetics complicates what Marcuse calls given realities through a restless and critical imaginary attuned to the potential of the negative, a potential found, paradoxically, in privation, rage, failure, confusion and conflict. In addition, we will explore the ways in which this negative potential aspires towards something revolutionary and utopic calling for sentient shifts both in our aesthetics and in our politics. Primary authors will include: Piri Thomas, Reyna Grande, Ernesto Mestre-Reed, Junot Diaz, and Iris Gomez. We will also read secondary literature by Theodore Adorno, Emmanuel Levinas, Frantz Fanon, Edward Said, Judith Butler, Michael Taussig, Mary Pat Brady, Fred Moten, Lyn Di Iorio Sandin, Patricia Gherovici, Jose Munoz, Siane Ngai, Sandra Ruiz, Cathy Park Hong, and Nicole Guidotti-Hernandez.

sections.title: After Afrofuturism: Futures of Black Speculation
sections.description: Afrofuturism attempts to articulate a speculative counter politics centered in cultural production organized around the radical fact that, as the artist Alisha B Wormsley so bluntly states, “there are Black people in the future.” This class investigates what comes after Afrofuturism, what kinds of speculation obtain once Wormsley’s challenge is taken as a given. We will accomplish this by engaging in recent cultural production that involves a (re)turn to what I’m calling Black archival speculation and what others describe as critical fabulation, afro-fabulation, and the Black Archival turn. These overlapping terms describe a desire to make legible a past that may not have existed as such through the creation of speculative texts that link unaccounted for resistance then to the full emancipation of Black life now. These fantastical imaginings—think Jesmyn Ward’s Sing Unburied Sing; Ryan Coogler’s Sinners; and Nickel Boys, both the Pulitzer Prize winning novel and the Academy Award nominated film—alongside critical interventions by Richard Iton, Saidiya Hartman, Tavia Nyong’o Brigette Fielder, and others transcend the generic expectations of sci-fi through its exploration of a (previously unknowable?) speculative past with all that this implies about both the Black critical imagination and the Black radical tradition.

sections.title: Urban Literacies
sections.description: This course asks students to investigate how literacies shape and guide community members in urban locations. If we envision literacy as a way that people read, write and interact with the world, how might the aspects of Urban Literacies influence the ways students in metropolitan environments learn, and consequently impact their local communities and a larger world? We will explore theories of Urban Literacies and how those theories directly impact our contemporary landscape. This will require us to interrogate how the acts of reading, writing, critically thinking and communicating shift based on various locations and urban epicenters over time. This course will also explore how technological advancements have changed the ways we interface with ideas of literacy.

sections.title: The Freedom Party: Liberation Aesthetics
sections.description: An inquiry into the long history of thinking about the aesthetic as a modality of liberation. The aesthetic is often under erasure (Hal Foster’s The Anti-Aesthetic, Terry Eagleton’s The Ideology of the Aesthetic), only to find reclamation as an emancipatory category (Tina Campt, Rita Felski). We’ll take up the question of art’s relation to revolution as raised in many traditions and from various perspectives, from Friedrich Schiller to Carrie Mae Weems. Can the aesthetic be social movements’ advance-guard or at least sidekick, or is it always their graveyard? What inclines aesthetic practice in the direction of political change? And is that change necessarily for the good (any number of MAGA poets running around these days)? Art (and debates about whatever that is) as inherently revolutionary (cf. Herbert Marcuse’s The Aesthetic Dimension) as opposed to art as quietist and escapist, or a bourgeois ruse (Eagleton); protest versus immanence, movement art over against movement understandings of all art. Questions certain to arise include “post-critique” celebrations of textual pleasure or surface reading; the (eternal) return of close reading (Johanna Winant, Jonathan Kramnick); the aesthetic as a space for the critique of sovereignty (Fred Moten, José Muñoz’s uses of Ernst Bloch); political embraces of form (Caroline Levine, Anna Kornbluh); the encounter of the literary and infrastructures like the postwar creative writing program and Amazon (Mark McGurl, Dan Sinykin); museum studies and the politics of installation; and whole new refunctionings of form as political intervention (J Dilla’s math, Taylor Swift re-recording her own catalogue, Arthur Jafa’s arrythmia, Kevin Everson’s dreadpan, Kara Walker’s anarchitecture). And there’s always still Adorno’s Aesthetic Theory to contend with. Other matters likely: the relation of parties to The Party (is there a DSA aesthetic worth defending?), the aesthetics of play, the question of ideology, psychoanalytic understandings of the creative act, the political unconscious, the role of art in emergent revolutionary formations such as the Paris Commune and conversely the revolutionary potential of apparently anodyne formations such as the dance floor. Other possible readings: Sigmund Freud, Leon Trotsky, Sergei Eisenstein, Walter Benjamin, D.W. Winnicott, Roland Barthes, John Berger, Susan Sontag, Fredric Jameson, Stanley Cavell, Greil Marcus, Sianne Ngai, Lauren Berlant, Kobena Mercer, Douglas Crimp, Wayne Koestenbaum, Claire Bishop, Nathaniel Mackey, Amber Musser, among others, with plenty of textual sites and examples.

sections.title: Archiving Queerness
sections.description:
Collecting, Finding, and Interpreting Artifacts of the Intersectional and the Marginalized In the boxes and folders of archives, objects appear inanimate and inert. Yet, as Bruno Latour claims, these types of quasi-objects or "actants" have an agency in human lives. They have often unacknowledged forces in how the world (i.e. ideologies) and the word (i.e., discourses) get shaped and conserved (or reformed and revolutionized). Archival artifacts offer a particular approach to Latour's actor network theory because, rather than just one snapshot of a specified moment in history, they allow a more expansive view over geographic areas and an extended longitudinal understanding over multiple generations. In this course, will collectively and collaboratively do four things (maybe a few other side tasks as well):

revisit some of the 20th-century collectors of artifacts who made research possible for archival researchers today.

critically examine the archives (the physical spaces), the archivization (the curation of chosen materials), and the archiving (the organization of materials once deposited). We will consider who and what gets into collections and then how their archival organization affects their usage.

visit some New York archives to explore what memory treasures they hold and how researchers might use them for divergent means and investigations.

spend some time choosing, viewing and analyzing primary archival artifacts to rehearse how to inscribe, interpret and integrate their meaning into our scholarship.

While we will focus upon literacy objects that have impacted 20th-century Queer and other marginalized communities for the purposes of shared analytic exercises together, students will have the freedom to choose and curate their own "exhibit" of objects to study, unpack, and write about.

sections.title: Syntax II
sections.description: This course lays the foundation for current Minimalist theory. It examines the empirical and conceptual motivations for the paradigm shift from Government-Binding theory to Minimalism and familiarizes students with recent developments in the Minimalist Program.By the end of this course, students should be able to:1. Understand the conceptual and theoretical motivations for Minimalist theory;2. Have access to the primary literature employing Minimalist theory; and3. Be proficient at engaging in syntactic argumentation within the Minimalist framework.

sections.title: Foundational Issues in Linguistics
sections.description: The goal of this course is to provide and encourage discussion of foundationalissues in Linguistics. Training in the subdisciplines of Linguistics often starts withpre-established assumptions about the direction of inquiry, and the methods used to pursue it. But equally important to the results of inquiry is the motivation behind the commitments that shape it. In Linguistics these include commitments as to what the subject matter of Linguistics is, what constitutes knowledge of language, whatcounts as relevant data, and how data are best collected and modeled. In this course we provide a forum for discussing these issues. We will examine questionsconcerning the place of Linguistics in the cognitive sciences and concerning thevalidity of the empirical and analytical methods employed by linguists. As such, thecourse is aimed to strengthen the grounds that more specialized courses build on, by encouraging critical assessment of the assumptions that linguists make (or take for granted) in their research.

sections.title: Topics in Global Early Modern Studies
sections.description:
This interdisciplinary seminar offers a broad introduction to the material culture of the early modern world, with particular attention to the relationship between empire-building and the extraction/production and circulation of natural and manufactured goods. Readings will include studies of particular materials (pearls, shells, silver, silk, tobacco, etc.) and scholarship steeped in different cultural contexts in Africa, Asia, Europe, and the Americas. Approximately half of the class sessions will take place off-campus at museums, libraries, and galleries, where we will examine early modern objects firsthand and meet with curators, conservators, and art dealers. In addition to object-based research, we will also explore the possibilities and limitations of using archival documents, published texts, and artistic representations as sources for writing about material culture.

To prepare for the first class meeting, please read the following two articles: Jules David Prown, “Mind in Matter: An Introduction to Material Culture Theory and Method,” Winterthur Portfolio, 17: 1 (1982), pp. 1-19, and Byron Ellsworth Hamman, “The Mirrors of Las Meninas: Cochineal, Silver, and Clay,” The Art Bulletin 91: 1-2 (2010), pp. 6-35.

This class fulfills one of the two core course requirements for the certificate in Global Early Modern Studies. Students from all programs are welcome; no previous experience is required or expected. No overtallies will be permitted, since class size must remain manageable for field trips; requests to audit will be considered if any seats remain open in the first week of the semester.

sections.title: Seminar in Interdisciplinary Studies
sections.description: The Seminar in Interdisciplinary Studies is required for all MALSstudents. Students will consider a range of disciplinary andinterdisciplinary approaches to academic study. Students areexpected to take this class in their first or second semester in theprogram. This course presents interdisciplinary method as a tool for academicstudy. As a topics class, each faculty who teaches the course will choose a subject of study related to their own research and design a syllabus that exploresthat topic through a range of disciplinary and interdisciplinary lenses. The class is designed to help students understand both disciplinary and interdisciplinary research, academic writing, and methodology. Students will write frequently inthis class and hone their written, oral, and analytic skills. It is also designed to support students as they develop their own disciplinary and interdisciplinaryresearch strategies. It will encourage them to begin thinking about their culminating thesis or capstone projects. One or more visiting faculty may be invitedto speak about their research, writing, and methodology.

sections.title: Topics in Translation Studies
sections.description: This seminar explores the history and theory of translation in the West. We will read and discuss major theoretical texts that have shaped the field of translation studies from Cicero and St. Jerome to Luther, Schleiermacher, Goethe, Benjamin, Jakobson, Borges, Venuti, Derrida, Berman, Spivak, Kilito and Apter among others in order to work our way through the various aesthetic, ethical and political questions raised by the practice of translation. Alongside these theoretical essays, we will examine key translations of literary and other texts as case studies that test the limits of these theories. At the end of the term, each student willredact a discussion of a specific translation theory or set of theories, an analysis of a specific translation or an original translation accompanied by a critical introduction. The class will be taught in English, but participants should have working knowledge of at least one language other than English, preferably French, German or Spanish.

sections.title: ST in Archaeology of the Classical Late Antique and Islamic Worlds
sections.description: This course introduces students to ancient, late antique, and early medieval letters and epistolography (the art of writing, circulating, and publishing letters). This course focuses on a single literary genre (letters) in a way that introduces students to wider research and reading methods relevant to premodern studies (ancient, late antique, medieval). Course readings will be in English; students with mastery of additional ancient/modern languages will be expected to incorporate these language skills in their research papers.

sections.title: The Political Ecology of Social and Environmental Justice
sections.description: This seminar examines classic and contemporary works on how social and environmental injustice is produced, understood, and resisted. It offers a broad overview of social theory relevant to the study of people-environment relations, tracing connections to contemporary environmental and climate justice scholarship and activism. Using a political ecology framework, we will pay attention to how the unequal distribution of environmental harms and benefits is produced at various scales and in locations across the globe, with a focus on how individuals and communities experience, understand, and respond to environmental degradation and climate change. We will consider a range of practices and theoretical understandings from north and south to explore ethical, methodological, and epistemological debates in political ecology, as well as political ecological factors (including spatial, cultural, technological, and psychological factors) that enable and constrain the just futures that scholars, activists, and communities imagine, as they reconfigure relations to nature, cities, the earth, and themselves through their struggles for social, epistemic, environmental, and climate justice.

sections.title: Seminar in Interdisciplinary Studies
sections.description: This course is an exploration of how contemporary fiction and nonfiction written and visual texts have responded to ongoing and impending climate crises. It is common knowledge that the rapidly warming planet already shapes global patterns of migration and will determine what human life looks like in coming years. And yet, the combination of negligent governance, industry recalcitrance, and proliferation of bad news about glaciers and wet bulb temperatures has led to a kind of generalized inertia or paralysis outside of activist circles about how to even contemplate climate crises. This course is a humanist approach to understanding the historical patterns of colonial extraction that have led to the present Anthropocene. In it, we will ask how history, philosophy, writing, cinema, and the arts can intervene to change and adjust how we think of the role of humanity on a rapidly changing planet. Students will be expected to participate in all in-person class sessions and write a final research paper or equivalent.

sections.title: Africana Studies: Global Perspectives
sections.description:
This course examines problems of existence and freedom posed by black life. We will explore how the racialization of people of African descent through the means of violence and oppression translates into an existential predicament addressing the human confrontation with hope and hopelessness, freedom, and human degradation, being and non-being. We will discuss the existentialist implications, challenges, and possibilities of black life in Africana literature, film, and music. How do cultural expressions of black people simultaneously engage being acted upon by the external forces of enslavement and racism, while acting against those forces? Through critical analyses of music, film, fiction, and contemporary events, this class will generate theoretical interventions embedded in the poetics and politics of (self) representation, freedom, and social constructions of black existence.

This seminar takes a critical look at carceral regimes in Africa, Asia, Latin America, North America, Europe and Australia in the past and present. We will explore carceral regimes through fiction, prison memoirs, testimony, ethnography, legal, policy, anthropological and other academic literature on imprisonment, detention and disappearance as State processes of domination and exclusion. One of our goals is to understand the ways in which carceral regimes and the official creation of historical truth(s) as well as definitions of crime and punishment reaffirm hegemonic structures and gendered Eurocentric colonial practices of exclusion and inequality.

sections.title: Special Topics in Public Scholarship
sections.description:
While there is a myriad of ways to do public scholarship, the GC holds a long radical tradition of research that is non-extractive, multidisciplinary, committed to the public good and rooted in Black Studies, Ethnic Studies and Queer Studies. Special Topics in Public Scholarship will honor these roots by exploring three interweaving pillars of knowledge production: Oral Histories, Archives, and Zines. We will study the work of feminist BIPOC oral historians, explore the politics of creating archives, and look at how radical histories interweave with Black feminist zine making practice. Students will work on a collective oral history project, learn how to curate oral histories for various archives, and deepen their zine-making practice.

This course introduces students to the art of cinema and to the language and study of film form. Over the course of the semester, students will analyze the stylistic components of filmmaking such as mise-en-scène, editing, cinematography, and sound; consider their historical deployment in the context of both narrative and experimental cinema, and within a variety of genres; and reflect on how these elements combine to generate meaning and structure the cinematic experience. Drawing on a range of theoretical perspectives, we will also consider the aesthetic properties of film in relation to authorship, industry, and ideology, and in connection to other media forms. One recurring concern will be with the medium-specific pleasures that cinema offers and the ways we qualify and translate our aesthetic experience of film into writing, including in the emergent mode of criticism known as the video essay. Students will be asked to respond to the readings and at-home screenings in a weekly one-page journals; to facilitate class discussion; and to complete a final paper or creative project. This class will fulfill a requirement for the Film and Media Cultures certificate.

sections.title: From UFOs to UAP: Disclosure and National Security
sections.description: We have entered a new era in how the American government treats UFOs, which are now referred to officially as Unidentified Anomalous Phenomenon (UAP). The 2021 Pentagon UAP Report not only acknowledged the reality of UFOs/UAP and called for their scientific study, but it also presented them as a threat to national security. This course will explore how the politics of disclosing the existence of UFOs entailed overcoming the longstanding “UFO taboo,” the reasons for changing the language from UFOs to UAP, the social implications of discovering that behind UAP there may be a non-human intelligence (NHI), and why the government “securitized” the concept by treating a scientific mystery as a national security threat. But do UAP really pose a threat, and if so, how should the government respond to that danger? Science fiction has often assumed the threat would be an external one of conquest or annihilation, which some theorists believe could lead to increased international cooperation by uniting humanity against a common enemy. We will consider that idea, along with alternative scenarios, including the worrisome possibility that the threat could lead to social collapse, as the State is unable to provide security against a technologically superior threat. We will explore how UAP expose the anthropocentric assumptions of modern state sovereignty, force societies to reimagine the concept of “security,” and challenge humanity to cooperate in new ways to deal with the political and scientific questions raised by the existence of UAP.

sections.title: Cinema Aesthetics
sections.description: Cinema Aesthetics provides students with the skills and vocabulary necessary to analyze cinematic texts by acquainting them with basic film techniques, strategies, and styles. Central topics may include narrative and non-narrative forms, mise-en-scene, composition and color, camera movement, editing, film sound and music genre, spectatorship, and seriality and other televisual modes. In addition, students will bcome familiar with a variety of historical and contemporary critical perspectives on film form as well as essential bibliographical sources and fundamentals of research in the field.

sections.title: Public Scholarship and Social Justice: Labor and Documentation in Asian NYC
sections.description:
This course introduces students to the intersections of public scholarship and social justice through the lens of Asian communities in New York City, with particular attention to labor organizing and working-class Asian communities. Interdisciplinary by design, students examine, analyze, and reflect on a range of scholars, artists, and activists who are committed to the vision of a more just world through their community-engaged, or public-facing work. Drawing on methodologies in oral history, participatory action research, public history, ethnography, public art projects and community-based archiving, the course pays special attention to how race, ethnicity, gender, class, and immigration status converge in the workplace and in the archive.

Case studies may include oral histories and art installations from Red Canary Song, participatory action research surveys used by the New York Taxi Workers Alliance and art projection and ‘placekeeping’ mapping used by Chinatown Art Brigade. We will also examine collections at the New York Public Library and Interference Archives. A central concern of the course will be the role of community documentation – from the mundane recounting of work tasks to the creation of worker education programs to the narratives formed through oral histories – to labor struggles in general.

By the end of the course, students will learn how to design and put into practice the framework for a successful public-facing, and/ or community-engaged research project.

sections.title: Film Theories
sections.description:
Wednesday, 5 pm - 9 pm, 3 credits, In person, Prof. Alexandra Juhasz, alexandra.juhasz@brooklyn.cuny.edu

Women and Film, a staple of film theory and history, is itself worthy of a theoretical and historical revisit. In Spring 2027, this class has the unique opportunity of joining with a sister class in Australia to investigate how women and film becomes the contemporary field of feminist (media) studies. Using a newly completed, co-edited DeGrutyer collection of the same name, Feminist (Media) Studies (2027), Alex Juhasz will team teach with Australian feminist artist and scholar Alex Martinis Roe to explore how feminist media and technologies shape our knowledge, relationships, and experiences of the world, and how scholars, artists, and activists transform them. Drawing on feminist, queer, Indigenous and anti-colonial practices in proximity to women, we will also expand our understanding beyond film, photography, and digital technologies to include bodies, materials, environments, archives and social relationships as media worthy of study. Through readings, discussions, screenings and collective studio workshops, we will experiment with different ways of study to consider how technologies can reproduce or challenge existing relations of power.

sections.title: Slavery and Social Status in Middle Eastern History
sections.description:
In this class, we will explore social, political, economic, legal, and cultural aspects of slavery in premodern Islamic history. Starting in the late antique Mediterranean, we will consider the emergence of a variety of forms of slavery in the Islamic Middle East, including military slavery and agricultural slavery, but focus especially on the enslavement of women. We will end with the complex relationship between Islam and transatlantic slavery and various ethical and political implications of the history of religiously validated enslavement. We will consider a range of sources, including legal material and popular literature. Prior knowledge of Middle Eastern or Islamic history is not required.

sections.title: American Cultures and Values
sections.description:
Tuesday, 6:30 pm - 8:30 pm, 3 credits, In person, Prof. David T. Humphries (DHumphries@qcc.cuny.edu)

This course will consider what American Studies is, how it emerged as a field, and what it can tell us about our present moment. The main goal is to make the course interesting, relevant, and most of all, useful for students working in American Studies or related fields, and the course design is meant to accommodate different levels of familiarity and experience. Students who are relatively new to American Studies will find that it provides a working overview of its history as an interdisciplinary field and an introduction to current debates and areas of particular interest; students who are farther along with their research projects will find opportunities to advance their scholarship by adding context and depth. The course is organized around three broad chronological themes: 1) Early Histories: Nation and Empire; Representation and Race 2) The Cold War: Media; Containment; Class 3) The Emerging Present: Technology; Gender; (Trans)Nationalism. For each unit, we will link theoretical, historical, and critical readings with specific cultural representations and artifacts – novels, memoirs, films, television shows, and music recordings and performances, among others. We will consider the roles of different institutions, political and economic configurations, and forms of technology in understanding how culture is produced, distributed, valued, and preserved. We will also investigate how culture is instrumental in identity formations and shaping group identities and how it can act as an active agent in changing the world. In order to allow students to explore their own interests and work on their academic research and writing, the course will include a number of shorter writing assignments, including responding to a keyword from one of the Keywords for American Cultural Studies volumes, writing a review of an artifact or event, creating and presenting an annotated bibliography, and drafting a proposal for a research project or submitting an excerpt from a longer work in progress.

sections.title: Selected Topics in Genocide, Mass Violence and Crimes Against Humanity
sections.description: The course will offer students in depth and critical knowledge of specific topics related to the study of Genocide and Crimes against Humanity, introducing them to a wide range of cutting-edge literature that builds on new methodological and interdisciplinary approaches. Some of the topics may include the study ofcausation, motivation, and resistance to genocide; the Holocaust, trauma, and memory studies; environmental history, ecological destruction, and genocide; colonialism, imperialism, racism, and genocide; the history of human rights; gender and genocide.

sections.title: Special Topics in Fashion Studies
sections.description:
This course examines dress as an expression of identity in the Islamic World. From luxury silks to patched wool, dress communicated the inner and outer states of its wearer. Communicating in a shared language stemming from both regional and religious sartorial codes, clothing represented social status, political allegiance, spiritual beliefs and personal tastes. Dress will be analyzed for both material properties and social context, with settings ranging from royal courts to subalterns in everyday life, from secret societies to Sufi mystics and chivalric guilds. Following summary lectures of the early and medieval periods, the course will focus on the early modern to modern eras, examining cross-cultural encounters, diplomatic exchange, and trade networks as contributors to fashion. Readings will include primary sources, travelogues, historiography and trade documents. Visual analysis includes depictions of dress in a range of visual media as well as object study.

sections.title: Thesis Workshop
sections.description: This course focuses on research and writing for the thesis. It is open to students in the MALS program who are working on their theses. Students will develop strategies for composing, drafting, and crafting their theses, which are extensive pieces of academic research. They will work on analyzing and synthesizing their materials in order to sharpen their approach to their scholarly topics. They will also work on developing their writing in logically framed and rhetorically convincing graduate-level prose. This course will have students consider issues such as clarity and coherence in their writing, as well as their uses of a range of stylistic conventions. Students will receive feedback from their peers as well as the instructor.Each student will be asked to research and write a substantial portion of their thesis by the end of the semester and some students will use this course as an opportunity to finish the entire project. Students will produce multiple drafts, consider the best organizational approaches for their projects, develop and hone the appropriate tone and voice for the project topic and the perceived audience, participate in peer review (inside and outside of class), develop strategies for building arguments that are supported by the evidence they have collected, and reflect upon their individual research and writing practices.

sections.title: Introduction to Global Modern and Contemporary Studies
sections.description: Colonialism and postcolonialism have profoundly shaped and continue to shape the modern and contemporary world. In this class, we will explore a range of case studies and theoretical pieces that ask questions about colonial and racial capitalism, indigeneity, gender and sexuality, carcerality, transnational organizing, social movements, borders, art, and other themes. We will focus on the experiences of marginalized and minoritized groups across the globe in order to understand the impact of colonial and settler colonial histories and legacies on their lives. We will also consider how the embodied axes of race, gender, class, sexuality, ability, and national origins determine the limits of material success, mental and physical well-being, access to healthcare and education, and struggle. The class will be organized thematically. Each week, we will examine a narrow set of questions that scholars have posed within a specific subfield through scholarly and creative writing as well as film and visual culture.

sections.title: Seminar in Special Topics: The Listening Guide: A Method for Narrative Analysis
sections.description: The Listening Guide is a qualitative narrative method employed to understand and analyze the interplay between people’s social worlds and their inner lives as lived experience. Using psychodynamic and critical theories that make the embodied psyche “visible,” the LG is especially well-suited to discover how people live with the disconnects between their own experience and ideologies about them that demonize, marginalize and dehumanizes. It has been used extensively to investigate questions anchored in social in/justice, taboo topics and social and relational conflicts and challenges. The method will be taught in a workshop format that spans the research process, from asking a real question, to the methodology of the LG, to conducting a LG interview, to learning and applying the specific steps of the method (including developing voices), and finally, to composing a case analysis that can be part of a paper, article and/or dissertation. Students will be proficient in using the LG for their own research.

sections.title: Comparative Revolutions
sections.description: What makes a revolution a revolution? Scholarship has recently moved away from social-scientific, Marxist-inspired explanations to approaches that explore how revolutionaries themselves understood what they were doing, how they interpreted their contexts, and how their ideas shaped their actions. With such questions in mind, we will look at and compare a number of revolutions, including the so-called “Glorious Revolution” of 1688, the American, French and Haitian Revolutions, the Revolutions of 1848, the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the recent Arab Spring. What characteristics did these revolutions share? What might they have learned and borrowed from each other? Is there something we can call a revolutionary “script”?
