sections.title: Writing Politics II
sections.description: Writing Politics II is the successor to Writing Politics I, although students may take it without taking the predecessor. The biggest difference is that we’ll focus more on writing for publication. The goal will be for each student to publish at least one, hopefully several, of the columns they write. We will start by coming up with a list of the publications that each student wants to target. We will then focus our reading on those publications, since in submitting to a particular publication, it's critical to understand its particular style and perspective. We will focus in more detail on how to make contact with particular editors at those publications and part of the assignments themselves will be figuring out (with my help) how to make the connections necessary to get your pieces seriously considered. I’ll tailor my guest speaker invitations to the particular publications students decide to target. If a piece is ready for publication on the first draft, I won’t ask for a rewrite. If the first draft suggests no hope of publication, I may suggest we choose a different topic rather than requesting a second draft. If there’s a danger of the window of opportunity on a certain subject closing, I may change the due dates for certain assignments. The goal is to give us maximum flexibility to increase the chances of publication. Because this course is more of a workshop than Writing Politics I, I may also bring in some of my own writing in concept or draft form and submit it to the same critical review that I give the students’ work. If there is student interest, I will also assign a longer essay (2000-4000 words) in addition to columns. Students who did not take Writing Politics I are welcome. I will likely set up a special session near the beginning to go over some of the basics about story organization and sentence structure that we covered in that class. And as the semester progresses, I will vary readings and assignments to make sure that students who need additional grounding in non-academic political writing get it. In the past, students who have not taken Writing Politics I have nonetheless thrived in Writing Politics II.

sections.title: The question of the narrator: thinking the boundaries of fiction in 20th century novels in French
sections.description:
*MALS students must take the course for 4 credits in order to count towards their degree.

This course considers the relation of the narrator to the narrated as an essential problematic in the theorizing of fiction. We will take a phenomenological approach as we read some key fictional texts in the modern history of fictional narration, texts which make their narration conspicuous or put into question the narrator as guarantor of the textual reality.

We will consider texts with incarnate narrators, as well as those without one. We will explore a renewed interest in modernity in various forms of fragmentation as we read novels whose structures are built out of a resistance to “central control”: novels which prefer intermittence over coagulation, and incompletion over unity. If the project of a narrative is often understood to organize lived experience into coherence, we will ask whether such coherence is not denied to us, here in this world: that is, does nararative produce melancholy in its apprehension of an inaccessible whole? and in what way might this be represented? We will pay particular attention to “unbalanced” texts, which do not equate understanding with a view from above, but plunge into what Maurice Merleau-Ponty calls “the forest of references.” In certain texts, we will seek out blanks and ellipses, markers of unnarrateable individual and collective trauma, which might suggest new problematics in the fictive representation of reality.

We will read literary texts, some in their entirety, others in excerpts, by Marcel Proust, Georges Perec, Michel Butor, Réjean Ducharme, Marguerite Duras, Kateb Yacine, Nathalie Sarraute and Edmond Jabès. We will also read other phenomenological, psychoanalytical, and narratological formulations of the relationship between author, narrator, character, and reader. Including those of Maurice Merleau Ponty, Gérard Genette, John Ruskin, Pierre Macherey, André Green, Nicolas Abraham and Maria Torok, Roman Jakobson, Marie-Chantal Killeen, and Abdullatif Kilito.

sections.title: Dismantling Interlocking Systems of Oppression: A DisCrit Orientation to Multiply Marginalized Students
sections.description: In this course, we will explore and apply DisCrit, a theoretical framework that combines tenets of Critical Race Theory (CRT) and Disability Studies (DS) as an analytical tool to interrogate interdependent constructions of race and disability in American culture writ large as well as public education. Through the lens of DisCrit, we will consider such questions as: How do racism and ableism circulate interdependently in ways that reify the construct of “normal”? What material and psychological consequences emerge from being labeled as raced and disabled? What mechanisms operate within educational laws and policies to oppress multiply marginalized students in neutralized and invisible ways? How does DisCrit inform our understanding of the persistent overrepresentation of students of color in segregated special education contexts? Course participants will have the opportunity to apply DisCrit to their individual research interests.

sections.title: Challenge the divide between theory and practice: Developing collaborative research methods
sections.description:
Traditional Western modernist social science aims to put ideal, generalized theories into practice. However, our practical reasoning includes our relationships with unique situations and engages our unique imagination, memories, skills, and experiences. Practical wisdom develops in relationships with other practitioners, in practice, creating multiple possibilities for multiple goals. This course will support students in collaboratively developing research methods that challenge the divide between theory and practice, and, thus, between method and object in conventional social science.

The shift that this course aims to support, towards the inclusion of formerly excluded ways of knowing, is a shift that is anti-status quo and far-reaching. Students will read the work of, and hear guest lectures by, researchers who have developed methods that cross theoretical traditions, professions, generations, and modes of existence. These methods have been developed and described within the following areas: romantic science, slow science, vulnerable observation, native science, early childhood education and care, elder care, creativity studies, cultural psychology, performance studies, and feminist, queer, and neurodiverse history and philosophy of science.

Students will learn about and visit a longitudinal participatory design research study that is led by early childhood teachers and based in these teachers’ own forms of inquiry, as they develop these forms of inquiry in real time with the young children, artists, and imaginary characters in their classrooms. (The study’s methods are introduced in this TED Talk.) The international field of early childhood education and care is a particularly fruitful space for the development of situated, ethical, historical research methods because young children are experts at creating multiple possibilities for multiple goals.

sections.title: Black Feminist Approaches to Education Research
sections.description:
The seminar centers on Black feminist thought and methodology to critically examine educational theory, policy, and praxis. It is designed for students in the Urban Education Ph.D. program, though relevant to students across CUNY interested in social justice, critical race studies, and feminist theory.

This seminar builds on existing CUNY strengths in critical race studies and feminist scholarship by providing a dedicated space for Black feminist methodological praxis in education. By centering Black women's intellectual traditions and lived experiences, the course challenges and expands traditional research methods that often overlook or misrepresent the experiences of marginalized communities. It directly addresses the call for more substantive training in critical race and feminist methodologies in graduate programs.

This seminar offers an in-depth exploration of Black feminist approaches to education research. It covers foundational Black feminist theory, key methodological tools, and the ethical considerations of conducting research with and within Black communities. Students will engage with a transdisciplinary body of scholarship, develop critical inquiry skills, and design a research project that applies Black feminist principles to an educational topic of their choosing.

sections.title: Urban Literacies
sections.description: This course asks students to investigate how literacies shape and guide community members in urban locations. If we envision literacy as a way that people read, write and interact with the world, how might the aspects of Urban Literacies influence the ways students in metropolitan environments learn, and consequently impact their local communities and a larger world? We will explore theories of Urban Literacies and how those theories directly impact our contemporary landscape. This will require us to interrogate how the acts of reading, writing, critically thinking and communicating shift based on various locations and urban epicenters over time. This course will also explore how technological advancements have changed the ways we interface with ideas of literacy.

The course is often team-taught, and in addition to a standard textbook, utilizes a variety of readings, oral presentations and research critiques designed to introduce students to the methods and data of these disciplines.Completion of Neuroscience I would be highly desirable. An emphasis on interdisciplinary work, which is characteristic of contemporary neuroscience, is an important feature of the course.

sections.title: Neuroanatomy
sections.description: This course will provide students with an overview of the structure and function of the nervous system and its subdivisions. It will introduce students to the organizational structure of the human brain, includeing slide material of gross neuroanatomy, cerbral vasculature, spinal organization, and internal structure from medulla to cortex. Functional system mini-lectures are also provided for the sensory and motor systems, the thalamus, hypothalamus, basal ganglia, limbic system, cerebellum and cortex. Neuroanatomical mapping of major neurochemical systems and their receptors is also proviced. Course expectations inlude both visuo-spatial and written fluency of the material.

sections.description: Students will be under the supervision of a licensed psychologist as the course instructor for all activities. The supervisor will have expertise in Neuropsychology. Students will interact directly with patients who have various neurological, psychiatric, and/or medical disorders. A number of practical skills such as building a professional CV, developing skills of presenting and publishing research, network building, jobs search, communication skills and time management are addressed. Relevance to student’s own evolving interests, skills, and professional standards are emphasized. This class uses a seminar format in which students meet with the faculty in Human Development and invited speakers. These weekly seminars serve three functions. sections.title: Contemporary Theory
sections.description: This course is designed to provide you with a thorough survey of important theorists in the development of Western social theory. A concurrent aim is to consider postcolonial critiques of Eurocentric social theory and the ways it has shaped the discipline of sociology. In the process, we will develop our understanding of how classical theory has influenced contemporary thinking and how current theorists present a wide variety of critical and interpretive perspectives on the social world. However, the most important goal of this course is to provide you with a set of conceptual tools that you can use to shape your research agenda and enhance your scholarship. Given these objectives, the course is not simply an abstract exercise but hopefully one that brings theory alive and shapes your sociological vision.

sections.title: Social Movements
sections.description: This class on Social Movements will address power, inequality, and politics. We will consider forms privilege in society, the means by which subdominant groups organize to improve their situations, the ways in which dominant groups organize to stop them, and how others adopt social movement methods to work for change on their own behalf. Topics will include organizing, mobilization, recruitment, collective action, collective identities, strategies, tactics, measuring outcomes, and long-term impacts. The fundamental question is how do we bring about social change? We can approach this question as 1.Identify and name an issue; 2. Explain why it’s an issue; (framing) 3. Identify the stakeholders; appeal to their interests; (identity work) 4. Demonstrate to others that this is real; (framing, outreach) 5. Explain why it’s like this; (diagnostic framing) 6. Demonstrate that it can be different; (prescriptive framing) 7. Wait for people to refuse to help; (mobilization, networks) 8. Demand change; 9. Request change; 10. Fight for change; 11.Debate whether 10% of what you demanded is enough; 12. Get 10%; watch it get scaled back to almost nothing over time; 13. Start over; Or maybe, make progress.

sections.title: From Research to Action: Public Sociology in Practice
sections.description: This course focuses on publicly engaged sociology (often called public sociology) that seeks to fight inequality and injustice. The course tries to address a key problem in graduate school and sociological careers: most of us go into sociology because it helps illuminate problems in the world, but we are taught much less about how to address those problems and make change with our research. The class will do readings from three types of publicly engaged sociology – Reframing, Debunking, or Alarm Sounding; Institutionally Engaged; and Community Engaged – which differ in their goals and the implications for graduate school and early sociological careers. Key case studies will be the Stories and Numbers Project in Texas (advocating for and protecting transgender children, especially in Texas), and work on immigration. We will do deep dives into both substantive professional sociological work produced by publicly engaged sociologists – including analyzing their research design, questions, methods, and final written analysis – and into their publicly oriented products – including websites, expert witness work, public testimonies, and other disseminations. We will discuss cultivating and navigating research relationships with research participants, community-based organizations, institutions, government, or other entities. For class papers, students can use their own fieldwork or other publicly engaged research for their class papers, dissertation proposals, or other work product that helps move their work forward.

sections.title: Geographies of Peace & Conflict
sections.description: Scholarship on the dynamics of peace and conflict is in the midst of a geographic renaissance. Within the discipline of Geography, there is growing interest among political geographers in theorizing and exploring “geographies of peace.” At the same time, the interdisciplinary field of Peace and Conflict Studies is experiencing a “spatial turn” whereby geographic ideas are increasingly engaged. This seminar provides an overview of these parallel conversations and explores potential analytical frameworks and research methodologies for bringing them together.

sections.title: Qualifying Paper Seminar
sections.description: This year-long seminar is an opportunity to conduct original research that will result in a journal article (i.e. The Qualifying Paper) that is of publishable quality in a peer-reviewed academic journal. This seminar is required of all PhD students during the second year in the program. Over the course of two semesters, you will formulate a research question, develop a theoretical argument, design a research strategy, collect and analyze your data, interpret the results, and present your argument and findings in a precise and compelling narrative form. At the end of the Fall term, you will hand in a clearly developed research proposal with a research plan. At the end of Spring term, you will hand in a complete research paper that contributes to sociological knowledge and this draft will form the basis for your first single-authored peer-reviewed article for submission. The article can be based on either an empirically-oriented or a theoretically-oriented research project, as long as it is deemed to be of publishable quality. (For second year students only.)

sections.title: Qualitative Social Analysis
sections.description: This course provides applied training in demographic and econometric analysis. In particular, the course will focus on estimation of key demographic rates from observational data, including mortality and fertility; demographic indicators of population health; demographic/econometric decompositions of group differences and related approaches for analyzing inequalities and mechanisms; foundations of causal inference; and quasi-experimental designs relevant for demographic analysis, including difference-in-differences and instrumental variables. Besides engaging with lectures and class discussions of scholarly papers, students will perform hands-on data analysis throughout the course using Stata (with permission to use R or other software). Students should be comfortable with algebra and regression analysis.

sections.title: Social Statistics II
sections.description: The broad focus of this course will be on applications of multivariate analysis in social science research, including Multiple Regression, Multivariate Analysis of Variance/Covariance, Factor Analysis, Categorical Data Analysis, among other relevant topics. The goals of this course are to provide students with an understanding of the principles underlying commonly used multivariate analysis approaches within the field of Sociology. Specifically, students will 1) acquire an understanding of some fundamental concepts in multivariate statistics, 2) become proficient in the performance of corresponding statistical procedures, and 3) be able to appropriately communicate these statistical concepts and skills to academic and lay audiences.

sections.title: Religion and Politics
sections.description: This class will explore the relationship between religion and politics. These realms of life have by no means always and everywhere been regarded as separate, and they may influence each other in important ways. The course will pay close attention to Max Weber’s typology of the “world religions” and to the central sociological phenomenon of “secularization.” Taking a comparative-historical approach, we will examine the ways in which religion waxes and wanes over time and across space. We will also focus on the earthly needs and desires of believers that religions are meant to address, the many “varieties of religious experience” (William James), and the organizational forms taken by different religio-political movements. Students will be expected to participate in class discussions, to write three “reflection papers” on the weekly readings, and to write a final paper of 15-20 pages addressing some question or questions raised by the class readings and discussions.

sections.title: Environmental Justice Policies and Practices
sections.description: This course focuses on the distributional dimensions of environmental degradation and environmental protection globally, domestically and in New York City. We will explore the social processes that generate synergistic race and class stratification, and how they impact the distribution of ecological costs and benefits. Substantive areas of focus will include the class and racial segregation of urban neighborhoods, the siting of hazardous facilities in communities of color, unequal protection of environmental health, unequal distribution of urban environmental amenities, and climate injustice. The course will also examine the social origins and impacts of a distinct environmental justice movement that emerged from BIPOC and working-class communities that are most at risk from climate change. Both successes and ongoing struggles in the EJ movement will be explored, with emphasis on NYC.

sections.title: The Politics of Inequality
sections.description: This course will cover substantive developments, measurement issues, and a variety of analytic approaches across the social sciences. It focuses on both the substantive and analytical/methodological aspects of the relationship between politics and economic inequality. Specifically, the objectives are to become familiar with (1) the different levels of analysis involved in the study of the politics of inequality, opportunity, and redistribution, namely, the role of political institutions (i.e., parties, electoral systems, policy regimes, the media, etc.) on the one hand, and behavioral dynamics (e.g., individual beliefs, policy preferences, voting choices, and protest/social movements) on the other hand, in shaping political and economic outcomes, and (2) the strengths and weaknesses of various methodological approaches to analyzing institutional and behavioral processes, such as political economy, public opinion and survey research, experimental research, ethnography, and discourse/textual analysis. To accomplish these objectives, readings will be interdisciplinary and include theoretical texts at the start of the course and empirically-based, substantive and methodological studies employing quantitative (including experimental) and qualitative data and methods throughout the rest of the semester (though the balance may lean toward quantitative studies). Students will therefore learn both theoretical and methodological skills, and their interdependence, in the study of the politics of inequality, opportunity, and redistribution. We will also integrate the research on class inequality with ongoing research on other dimensions of inequality, such as gender and racial/ethnic inequality.

sections.title: Labor and Inequality in the U.S., Past and Present
sections.description: Designed as an introduction to recent sociological debates on labor and inequality, this seminar involves study and discussion of key texts on that topic. The course focuses primarily on the case of the USA, past and present. We will explore the causes and consequences of growing precarity and labor market polarization since the late 1970s, and the accompanying widening of class inequality. Other questions to be examined include the impact of recent labor market transformations on groups that were historically marginalized — especially women, people of color, and immigrants — and the recent widening of class inequalities within each of those groups. Implications of these changes for the organized labor movement will be examined as well.

sections.title: Global Immigrant Cities
sections.description: Global immigrant cities are crucial research sites for exploring the possibility of going “beyond” the nation-state and national society as traditional foci of migration research. This course asks the question of how immigrant-receiving global cities experience, respond to, and are transformed by the changing composition of their ethnic and racial populations. It will explore global immigrant cities’ histories of ethnic and racial difference; how their ideologies about diversity, pluralism, and multiculturalism have evolved and changed over time; the extent to which they incorporate (or not) their immigrants (including forced migrants and refugees); and the different economic, cultural, and political impacts that immigration has had on these places. Specific examples of cities will vary but will include geographically diverse places in both the Global North (e.g., New York City, London) and Global South (e.g., Lagos, Manila). The main focus will be on international comparison, and students will be trained in the use of comparative perspectives to illustrate similarities and differences between global cities. While a crucial dimension of globalization, the comparative study of migration also opens up fresh comparative and international perspectives on the urban experiences of immigrants.

sections.title: Social Policy and Socio-Economic Outcomes in Industrialized Countries
sections.description:
This course provides an introduction to cross-national comparative research, with a focus on socio-economic outcomes and on the policies and institutions that shape those outcomes. The course is organized around two databases available through LIS, a data archive located in Luxembourg, with a satellite office here at the Graduate Center.

LIS contains two main micro-databases. The Luxembourg Income Study (LIS) Database includes nearly 1000 micro-datasets from approximately 60 high- and middle-income countries. These datasets contain comprehensive measures of income, employment, and household characteristics. A smaller, companion dataset – the Luxembourg Wealth Study (LWS) Database – provides microdata on assets and debt. Since the mid-1980s, the LIS data have been used by more than 20,000 researchers – mostly sociologists, economists, and political scientists – to analyze cross-country and over-time variation in diverse outcomes such as poverty, income inequality, employment status, wage patterns, gender inequality and family structure.

Many researchers have combined LIS’ microdata with various macro-datasets to study, for example, the effects of national social or labor market policies on socio-economic outcomes, or to link socio-economic variation to national-level outcomes such as child well-being, health status, political attitudes and voting behavior. (The LIS and LWS data are accessed through an internet-based “remote-execution system”. All students are permitted to use the LIS microdata at no cost and without limit.)

1) Students will read and assess a selection of published studies based on the data.

2) Students will carry out an original piece of empirical research using the LIS or LWS microdata. That work will culminate in a term paper.

While there are no formal prerequisites, students must have a working knowledge of basic statistics and beginner-to-intermediate capacity in one of these programming languages: SAS, SPSS, Stata, or R.

Neither statistics nor programming will be part of the course's curriculum. Extensive documentation about the data, self-teaching materials, and instructional videos are available on the LIS website.

All MA students must seek permission from the instructor before registering. MA students should email the instructor with a brief description of their relevant background.

sections.title: Sociology of Culture
sections.description: We will study the main theoretical approaches (classical and contemporary) to understanding the cultural dimension of social life and will do so by seeing how far they can illuminate a range of case studies of cultural areas. These case studies include film/movies; music; political views/attitudes; museums/concert halls/theme parks; theater/Broadway; fashion; art; religion; sports; nightlife, clubs, bars-restaurants; architecture; public statues; the internet/online entertainment/social media/the high-tech economy/AI; television; literature, food, education/schools, and the coronavirus. The theoretical perspectives include: Veblen and status theory, Marxism, the Frankfurt school, Durkheim, the mass culture school, “creative culture” approaches, consumption theorists, the British school of cultural studies (e.g. Raymond Williams, Stuart Hall), Modernism and post-Modernism, the “popular culture” versus “high culture” debate including theories of “homemade” culture, cultural capital theory, the sociology of boundaries and cultural identity theory, Richard Florida and “creative class”/creative production approaches, Internet and Social Media theorists, debates over public policy towards the arts including theories of cultural controversy. Students will also be encouraged to develop new theories.

This seminar approaches feminist theory and method through whole books rather than excerpts. We read four full-length works by feminist authors who build theory from lived experience, whether the experience of the women they work with or their own: women porters in Accra, forensic nurses and survivors of sexual assault in the United States, workers and residents of a tax-haven economy in the US Virgin Islands, and a memoirist writing about her own body. Each book is paired with a shorter text that gives us a conceptual, methodological, or genealogical lens, and each unit ends with a conversation/podcast/interview with/by the author.

We ask how feminist scholars write lives, how they decide whose stories are told, by whom, and with what obligations. Themes include African and Black feminist theory, the erotic as knowledge, care and violence, racial capitalism and gendered labor, embodiment and fatness, and the ethics of ethnographic and autobiographical storytelling. Students learn to read a book as an argument, a method, and a piece of craft, and to think about how they might write their own work.

sections.title: Race, Gender, and Criminal Justice
sections.description: This interdisciplinary course examines how gender and race shape social experiences and inequalities in contemporary society. The course draws on concepts, theories, and current scholarship from a variety of disciplines, including sociology, criminology, criminal justice, gender studies, history, and economics. Topics may include mass incarceration and justice-involved women; gendered migration; sexual victimization and gender-based violence; drug use, mental illness, and the “War on Drugs” in the United States; educational inequality and achievement; reproductive rights; capitalism and labor markets; and contemporary social movements, among others. By the end of the course, students will gain a deeper understanding of major contemporary social problems and the ways in which race, gender, class, and other social identities shape individual experiences, life opportunities, and achievements. Students will learn to critically analyze social issues through an intersectional lens, evaluate current policies, and consider alternative approaches to promoting social justice, equality, and social change. The course will culminate in student presentations on topics of their choice related to gender, race, and social justice.

sections.title: Neapolitans Narratives, from Elena Ferrante to Gomorrah: Literature, Cinema, Television
sections.description:

Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan tetralogy shined a spotlight on an Italian city which had long exercised the imagination of philosophers, literati and visual artists. Called by Walter Benjamin a porous city for its theatrical architecture and for its ‘inexhaustible law of life’, Naples is not merely setting but protagonist in recent literary, cinematic, and televisual texts. Starting from the critical reflections of Benjamin, Antonio Gramsci and Franco Cassano, this course will discuss the complex portrayal of contemporary Naples in three different modules: the first and most extensive will center on Elena Ferrante’s entire literary production, while the second will analyze the cinematic works of a group of directors strongly associated to Naples: Mario Martone, Paolo Sorrentino, and Matteo Garrone. The seminar will conclude with a module that examines the representation of Naples in three series: the adaptations of Ferrante’s My Brilliant Friend and Roberto Saviano’s Gomorrah, and the breakout hit The Sea Outside. The course will be conducted in English.

sections.title: Reading Annie Ernaux
sections.description:
THIS IS A SEVEN-WEEK COURSE. THIS COURSE WILL BE OFFERED FOR THE FIRST SEVEN WEEKS OF THE SEMESTER.

In her 2022 speech upon receiving the Nobel Prize in Literature, Annie Ernaux describes what she felt when she first studied literature: “Literature was a sort of continent which I unconsciously set in opposition to my social environment. And I conceived of writing as nothing less than the possibility of transfiguring reality.” Since 1974, Annie Ernaux has published books in several genres: novel, memoir, personal diaries, exterior diaries, dialogues and interviews. She writes in the first person as a woman from the working classes who identifies as a “transfuge,” a class defector. The books, slim in format, are also meditations on recurrent and often interlocking themes: love, death, sex, identity in the social world—a practice that Ernaux named "autosociobiographie"–and always, the stakes of writing itself. Looking back now over Ernaux’s long career, what will we make of her project?

During a seminar of seven weeks, we will read Ernaux’s work across several genres. Students may read in English or in French, though class discussion will be in English.

sections.title: Desire’s Politics: History and Theory
sections.description:
INSTRUCTOR PERMISSION REQURIED. Students must contact Professor Herzog directly to ask for permission. If the instructor allows you in the course, you must then ALSO forward that exchange to the WGS APO (msheehan@gc.cuny.edu) WITH YOUR CUNYFIRSTID NUMBER to obtain the necessary permission.

What can historians and others with adjacent curiosities learn from classics in the history of sexuality, a field that burgeoned from the 1990s onwards, and in what directions might the field go now? What value could potentially be gleaned from revisiting psychoanalysis, that by now 125-year-old, so oft-reviled but also oft-revised originary theory of desire? What even is the “it” that we call sexuality, what are its boundaries, and how can we theorize its relationship to other realms of existence? Initially for Europe and the U.S., but increasingly for every part of the globe, scholars not only investigated the ever-intricate interplay of laws and customs, values and practices surrounding abortion, contraception, eugenics, hetero- and homosexuality, marriage, orgasm, pornography and prostitution, sex advice and education, and sexual abuse and violence, but also demonstrated conclusively that, at least for modern history, there simply was no major phenomenon that could not be more fully and deeply understood if attention to the history of sexuality was brought to bear – from the Enlightenment and the French Revolution to industrialization and imperialism, from the world wars and the rise and defeat of fascisms to the Cold War and then the aftermath of communism. Any history of the present, however, would have to test that proposition anew. As a class, we will study historical, contemporary, and theoretical materials and identify fresh questions as well as preliminary answers. Instructor permission required.

Other topics will include how nations decide who can and cannot migrate, how citizenship is established, what factors shape policies and their implementation, the increased role of municipalities in making policy towards immigrants, refugee resettlement, and immigrant integration and deportation.

sections.title: Foundations of Queer Studies II – Praxis
sections.description: Building upon Foundations of Queer Studies I: Epistemologies, Foundations of Queer Studies II: Praxis explores the concept of praxis and its differentiation from theory, model, and framework. The course excavates how praxis operationalizes and puts theory into action. Students will survey distinctive (non)traditional methods. A deeper dive will move toward the “queering” of methodology and intersections with traditional investigative strategies often used within disciplines that inform LGBTQ studies such as literature, cultural studies, social sciences, history, humanities, women’s and gender studies, humanities, and sexuality studies. Course content will examine the implications of “queering” praxis on historical and current social change and cultural shifts in local, national, and global societies. Through applied areas such as health, law, education, business, and journalism, students will contrast praxis approaches and assess their utility to address queer-focused social justice issues. Students will formulate the expansive roles of ethics and reflection in “queering” methodology and “queering” praxis. While examining real-world praxis application to address LGBTQ issues, in an applied project, students will bridge epistemology to praxis. Students will critique if and how processes of praxis begin with theory and end with theory being reframed.

sections.description: Feminist Listening to Contemporary Music develops modes of feminist listening across a range of c20 and c21 music. Using intersectional critical tools, this course examines a wide repertory of music, including popular music (rock, R&B, hip-hop, jazz, blues, traditional/folk, country) and art music. It aims to develop your ability to hear, discuss, and respond to music and sound through lenses of gender/sexuality/race/ethnicity/ability/power. We will think about what it means to “do” feminist listening and how intersectional listening—a concept offered by the ethnomusicologist Allie Martin—can change our relationships to music, sound, and the world. Together we’ll develop a critical vocabulary and grammar for discussing and analyzing the effects and meanings of contemporary music as understood by twenty-first century listeners. Course readings include theoretical, analytical, musicological, poetic, and autobiographical texts drawn from music studies, feminist/gender/queer/trans studies, ethnic studies, Third World studies, anthropology, sociology, literary study, and visual art. Through close listening to an array of music and reading of texts, the course uses a variety of intersectional sieves, opening new vistas for understanding music, sound, and art in everyday life. sections.title: Oppression, Nonideal Theories of Justice, and Social Change
sections.description: Contemporary political philosophers have had shockingly little to say about to transition from this world to a more just one. Ideal theorists have assumed this is mostly an empirical question. But most nonideal theorists have also unintentionally sidelined the question by focusing on reparative justice. This course will examine normative questions raised by transitions out of injustice, with an emphasis on the particular injustice of oppression. Though readings will largely be drawn from contemporary Anglo-American political philosophy, we will also examine work on institutional design currently being developed by social movements that emphasize the need for “just transitions,” such as degrowth, ecoterritorial feminisms, anti-extractivist movements, and landless movements.

sections.description: Discourse Theory and Analysis focuses on expression as inter-action among individuals, groups, and institutions, and, most recently, also AI (LLMs). Guided by critical social theory and animated with qualitative and mixed methods, this course involves a way to study the tensions, echoes, and transformations inherent in diverse actors' expressive media around an issue of research interest. Relevant media for human development, well-being, and social change include personal narratives, policies, laws, images, curricula, memes, and digital systems. Students are encouraged to work on their own research projects and interests; readings, lectures, and workshops will also provide material for our consideration together. No prerequisite. Black Feminist Approaches to Education Research
sections.description:
The seminar centers on Black feminist thought and methodology to critically examine educational theory, policy, and praxis. It is designed for students in the Urban Education Ph.D. program, though relevant to students across CUNY interested in social justice, critical race studies, and feminist theory.

This seminar builds on existing CUNY strengths in critical race studies and feminist scholarship by providing a dedicated space for Black feminist methodological praxis in education. By centering Black women's intellectual traditions and lived experiences, the course challenges and expands traditional research methods that often overlook or misrepresent the experiences of marginalized communities. It directly addresses the call for more substantive training in critical race and feminist methodologies in graduate programs.

This seminar offers an in-depth exploration of Black feminist approaches to education research. It covers foundational Black feminist theory, key methodological tools, and the ethical considerations of conducting research with and within Black communities. Students will engage with a transdisciplinary body of scholarship, develop critical inquiry skills, and design a research project that applies Black feminist principles to an educational topic of their choosing.
